documents.abstract: This paper develops a framework for an AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison course by bringing together Byram’s intercultural communicative competence model, Vygotsky’s constructivism, and Huang et al.’s theory of cultural competence development. It identifies five interrelated course goals: cultural knowledge, cross-cultural practical ability, critical cultural awareness, AI collaboration literacy, and human-AI symbiosis awareness. To achieve these goals, three teaching strategies are proposed. First, content should be reconstructed through multimodal and professionally adapted resources; second, the learning process should be immersive and adaptive; third, assessment should be data-driven and multidimensional to evaluate the goals. The implementation conditions of these strategies are further discussed in terms of teacher AI competence, human-AI boundary negotiation, algorithmic bias mitigation, and differentiated task design. It provides a structured basis for AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison teaching and for future empirical testing of its effects.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across reproductive medicine, including semen analysis, sperm detection and selection, oocyte and embryo assessment, prediction of assisted reproductive technology outcomes, clinical decision support, and integration of multi-omics data. Large language models and generative AI are also emerging as tools for scientific writing, education, documentation, and research support. This review critically examines the current applications, clinical readiness, and research-integrity implications of AI in reproductive medicine. Although many models demonstrate promising performance in classification, ranking, or outcome prediction, the available evidence remains predominantly retrospective, task-specific, and derived from single-center or internally validated datasets. High technical performance does not necessarily translate into improved cumulative live birth, patient safety, cost-effectiveness, workflow efficiency, or equitable clinical outcomes. Important barriers include dataset heterogeneity, limited external and prospective validation, inadequate calibration assessment, data leakage, algorithmic bias, limited interpretability, privacy and cybersecurity risks, and vulnerability to performance drift. Generative AI introduces additional concerns, including fabricated references, inaccurate scientific summaries, undisclosed contributions, confidentiality breaches, and the generation or alteration of images that may be misrepresented as empirical evidence. Responsible translation therefore requires transparent reporting, independent temporal and geographic validation, subgroup and fairness analyses, prospective clinical-impact evaluation, preservation of data and model provenance, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Current international guidance further emphasizes that AI systems cannot qualify as authors and that accountable human researchers must verify generated content and disclose material AI use. AI should presently be regarded as an assistive technology that augments, rather than replaces, embryologists, clinicians, and researchers. Future progress will depend on multicenter prospective studies using patient-important outcomes, design-appropriate reporting frameworks, risk-based regulatory oversight, and clearly defined human accountability throughout the AI lifecycle.

documents.abstract: In Brazil's 2026 presidential first round, the ballot box contradicted most polls: 136 of the 161 national polls showed Lula da Silva ahead, but Flávio Bolsonaro finished first. Public debate swung between fraud claims and the margin of error, and no open resource let students verify either with real data. Following a design and development approach, this study used generative AI (GenAI) under human curation to build the Atlas of the Errômetro, an open educational resource in which each section lets users learn, question, and test how registered polls compared with the official result. Data on 1,297 registrations came from the Superior Electoral Court, results were located through documentary search, and automated programs gathered report status and 130 compliance audits. The 901 included polls were compared with the ballot using the declared margin, the A index, the audit category, and a retrospective revealed-efficiency measure. Only 5.9% of the 896 comparable polls fell within their margin (31.5% in the last three days), against about 92% expected under unbiased random sampling; errors were systematic, with 530 nominally significant deviations toward Lula against 82 toward Flávio; Compliant or Caution polls erred less (7.1 versus 8.1 percentage points) but leaned toward Lula as often; and declared cost showed no detectable association with accuracy, with random-sample equivalence of about 2.3%. Each finding became an inquiry users can repeat, with activities, exam-style items, and games verified by automated tests. This first design cycle shows feasibility; effects on learning remain to be evaluated.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. Results Of 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). Conclusions While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, making accurate and efficient risk stratification essential across the care pathway. Numerous tools support emergency triage, disease assessment, procedural decision-making, long-term prevention, atrial fibrillation management, and evaluation of functional status, but no single model is applicable across all clinical settings or populations. This clinician-oriented review categorizes and critically compares commonly used cardiovascular assessment and risk-prediction tools, including History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin, Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events, and Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction for emergency triage; Agatston, Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, and Synergy Between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with Taxus and Cardiac Surgery for anatomical and clinical assessment; European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation, Society of Thoracic Surgeons, and Revised Cardiac Risk Index, for procedural risk; and Framingham, the pooled cohort equations implemented in the Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Risk Estimator, Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2, QResearch Cardiovascular Risk Algorithm 3, and Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs for long-term prediction. Congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75, diabetes, stroke/transient ischemic attack (2 points), congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 (2 points), diabetes, stroke/TIA (2 points), vascular disease, age 65–74, sex category (female), and hypertension, abnormal renal/liver function, stroke, bleeding history, labile international normalized ratio, elderly, drugs/alcohol, are discussed in the context of atrial fibrillation, alongside New York Heart Association and the Seattle Angina Questionnaire as measures of functional status and quality of life. For each tool, we examine its clinical purpose, principal variables, strengths, limitations, practical applications, and areas of overlap. Differences in implementation across healthcare systems and patient populations are considered to support context-appropriate selection. Persistent limitations include poor standardization, reliance on data that may be unavailable in resource-constrained settings, limited transportability, and incomplete integration into clinical workflows. Greater harmonization, external validation, digital automation, and the careful incorporation of biomarkers and artificial intelligence may support more accessible, dynamic, and personalized cardiovascular risk assessment.

In high-stakes domains such as finance, critical information evolves through multi-party interaction. Recovering these changes and their sources is fundamental to reliable speech understanding. Existing speech benchmarks focus on transcription, local understanding, and turn-level state prediction, leaving joint decision evolution across speakers insufficiently evaluated. We introduce DecisionTraceBench, a speech state-tracking benchmark for Decision-Critical Information State Tracking (DCIST). It jointly evaluates decision event sequences, speaker attribution, scope, and temporal evidence, using trajectory-level F1 to measure complete event-chain recovery. Our dataset comprises Chinese financial dialogues involving two to four speakers, with 100.39 hours of synthetic audio and 8.61 hours of human-performed recordings. On a fixed cohort of human-performed recordings, five cascaded systems and two direct-audio models achieve DCIST scores of 5.73% to 21.35%. Ablations with speaker-labeled reference scripts and no temporal localization requirements yield a maximum score of only 38.72%. Audio perturbation experiments further show that overall transcription error rates do not adequately reflect complete trajectory recovery. These findings reveal limitations in jointly understanding information provenance and state evolution, providing a benchmark for evaluating decision-process understanding and decision traceability in high-stakes speech applications.

Abstract Background Bronchoscopic biopsy in elderly patients with Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (AECOPD) presents high procedural risks. This case study analyzes the critical care nursing trajectory of an 76-year-old patient who survived a massive endobronchial hemorrhage and subsequent in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) during an interventional procedure. Resentation An 76-year-old male with severe COPD (FEV1 40% predicted) and hypertension underwent diagnostic bronchoscopy. Immediately following mucosal biopsy, the patient developed massive hemorrhage (approx. 300 mL), leading to acute asphyxia and pulseless electrical activity (PEA). The critical care nursing team initiated a rapid response, facilitating emergency tracheal intubation and localized hemostasis using epinephrine irrigation. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after 6 min of advanced life support. Nursing interventions The nursing management focused on three critical phases: (1) Crisis Resource Management (CRM): utilizing rapid situational awareness to clear the airway and coordinate multidisciplinary resuscitation; (2) Post-ROSC Stabilization: implementing lung-protective ventilation and precise cuff pressure titration (25–30 cmH 2 O) to prevent re-bleeding and ventilator-associated complications; and (3) Secondary Prevention: managing the delicate balance between necessary anticoagulation for cardiovascular comorbidities and the risk of recurrent pulmonary hemorrhage during the recovery phase. Conclusion This case report documents the successful resuscitation of an 76-year-old male with severe AECOPD (FEV1 40% predicted) who developed massive endobronchial hemorrhage (~ 300 mL) and in-hospital cardiac arrest (pulseless electrical activity) during diagnostic bronchoscopy. Detailed preoperative risk stratification, intraoperative crisis resource management, and post-ROSC intensive care nursing interventions are described and analyzed. A comprehensive geriatric assessment, complete resuscitation parameters, functional outcomes, and a comparative discussion with existing literature on bronchoscopy-related airway hemorrhage are provided. A nine-phase nursing decision-making framework for high-risk bronchoscopy in elderly AECOPD patients is proposed. This report highlights the critical role of nursing-led situational awareness, structured crisis management, and dynamic hemodynamic titration in navigating catastrophic cardiopulmonary events in high-risk elderly populations. Clinical trial number not applicable.

The emergence of artificial intelligence in primary education is changing the way teaching materials are structured, information is acquired, and learning decisions are made. These changes require a reconsideration of the teacher's position, particularly when system recommendations begin to influence assessments of children's needs and abilities. This article aims to redefine the role of primary school teachers through the relationship between pedagogical agency, knowledge authority, and educational ethics. The review employs a critical narrative literature approach to 19 selected publications from 2021–2026, encompassing empirical research, research reviews, conceptual articles, and policy documents that provide open access or official download facilities. The literature is reviewed based on educational context, type of evidence, conceptual contributions, and limitations of its application to primary schools. The synthesis shows that the benefits of AI depend on learning objectives, professional judgment capacity, and institutional support. Teacher agency requires the authority to review, modify, and reject system recommendations. Knowledge authority rests on the ability to explain the basis for a claim and guide the examination of evidence. Educational ethics need to be embodied in data protection, equitable access, child engagement, and the sharing of responsibilities. The article proposes the role of teachers as learning designers, knowledge assessors, relational facilitators, and advocates for children's interests. This reconceptualization requires case-based professional development and school governance that does not center all technological risks on teachers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Aeon Mundi is a collection of adaptive furnishings and robotic tools designed to connect small-plot, rotational food growing with the everyday life of homes, civic buildings, and shared public spaces. Its six pieces support a connected journey from cultivation and habitat care to harvesting, processing, and transport. Workstations, companion seating, and autonomous carts combine adjustable ergonomics with robotic assistance for moving crops, trays, and tools, keeping people involved at each stage. A common material language unites the collection: polished solid-cast mycelium in natural, vegetable-pigmented hues; sustainably loomed bamboo upholstery; rounded, repairable forms; and fine luminescent accents that respond to work phases. Embedded spatial displays offer abstract, user-invoked cues. Together, these elements frame food production as an accessible part of shared daily life and propose a design system for exploring how productive landscapes and human-centered technology can coexist.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. We conclude with actionable implications emphasizing mitigations beyond model-level safeguards such as content filtering: age assurance, consent verification for depiction, safety-by-design UX constraints, incident disclosure norms, and auditing regimes targeting developmental risk. Privacy-minimized annotations, a codebook, and documentation are available at https://github.com/The-Responsible-AI-Initiative/KidAID.

No-code development platforms integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide opportunity for non-technical users, like entrepreneurs, to innovate in software development. However, they still necessitate a level of coding proficiency to use effectively. A case study of building a travel mobile app with low and high tech prompts in an LLM-based no-code development platform explores how to support non-technical users by mapping technical capabilities to product needs described in plain English. The low tech prompts yield variable results in successful feature implementation and can mimic functionality instead of using the needed technical capabilities. The findings from this evaluation inform prompting guidelines, supporting non-technical users in executing their business and product needs. Mapping user concepts to underlying technical capabilities can be used as a framework to support usability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for programming applications.

The main aim of this study was to find the connection between perceived university fairness, resilience and academic engagement among university students in Karachi, Pakistan. The cross-sectional correlational design was used, 500 young adults (males = 121, female = 376, other = 3) aged 18 to 26 and above were selected from public, private and federally chartered universities through convenience sampling. The participants answered the University Fairness Questionnaire, Brief Resilience scale and Academic Engagement scale having 3 sub-scales including behavioral, cognitive and anxious engagement. The results via statistical analysis demonstrated that perceived university fairness has a significant negative correlation with behavioral engagement, and cognitive engagement, whereas it positively correlates with anxious engagement. Resilience showed positive correlation with cognitive engagement, a significant negative correlation with anxious engagement and no significant relationship with behavioral engagement. A significant negative correlation was found between perceived university fairness and resilience. The outcomes suggest that higher perceptions of university unfairness are linked to lower resilience and academic engagement, also increasing anxious engagement among higher education students. The research highlights the value of encouraging fairness, boosting resilience and improving student engagement alongside psychological well-being in university settings.

Precision livestock farming increasingly relies on intelligent monitoring systems to improve animal health, welfare, and farm productivity. However, conventional cloud-centric approaches often face challenges related to data privacy, communication overhead, network dependency, and real-time decision-making. This study proposes a Federated Learning (FL) and Edge-AI framework for distributed livestock health monitoring that integrates Smart Neck Collar sensing, edge computing, MQTT-based communication, and a hybrid Gradient Boosting–Long Short-Term Memory (GBoost-LSTM) prediction architecture. The proposed framework enables local preprocessing, model training, and inference at participating farms while supporting collaborative model learning without transferring raw livestock sensor data to a central server. A simulation-based federated evaluation was designed using livestock health data collected from 150 dairy cows across seven districts of Punjab, India. The proposed framework was compared with previously evaluated centralized machine-learning approaches to assess its predictive performance. The simulated FL-GBoost-LSTM model achieved an accuracy of 95.12%, precision of 93.48%, recall of 88.21%, and F1-score of 90.76% under the evaluation configuration described in this study. The results indicate that federated collaborative learning can provide competitive disease-prediction performance while retaining data locally at participating farms. In addition, the proposed edge-based architecture is designed to reduce dependence on continuous cloud connectivity and support localized health-status assessment. Because the present evaluation is simulation-based and does not constitute a field deployment, the reported communication, latency, privacy, and scalability benefits should be interpreted as framework-level findings rather than validated operational outcomes. Future work will focus on real-world multi-farm deployment, systematic non-IID evaluation, formal privacy-enhancement mechanisms, and comprehensive benchmarking of computational, communication, and energy requirements. Proposed a Federated Learning and Edge-AI framework for distributed livestock health monitoring across geographically separated dairy farms. Integrated Smart Neck Collar sensing, MQTT-based communication, edge computing, and hybrid GBoost-LSTM prediction within a unified architecture. Simulated collaborative model training across distributed farm-level datasets while retaining raw livestock data locally. Achieved 95.12% accuracy, 93.48% precision, 88.21% recall, and 90.76% F1-score under the reported simulation-based evaluation configuration. Compared the proposed federated framework with previously evaluated centralized livestock disease-prediction models to assess predictive performance. Identified communication efficiency, edge inference, non-IID data handling, privacy enhancement, and real-world deployment as key areas requiring further experimental validation.

This work proposes a high-speed, power-efficient, and fault-tolerant finite impulse response (FIR) filter architecture by integrating Vedic mathematics, reversible logic, and error-correction coding into an FPGA-based framework for machine-learning accelerators. A 16-tap FIR filter is implemented on a Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGA using the Urdhva-Tiryakbhayam Vedic multiplication technique with reversible Peres and controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates and a reversible look-ahead carry adder (LACA), enabling parallel computation with reduced information loss. A Hamming-code-based error correction code (ECC) module is incorporated to detect and correct single-bit soft errors without the hardware overhead associated with triple modular redundancy (TMR). Synthesis results demonstrate a propagation delay of 30.932 ns and power consumption of 2.645 mW, achieving a 5.57% latency improvement over an multiple constant multiplication (MCM)-based FIR baseline while providing single-bit fault correction. The proposed architecture demonstrates its suitability as a replacement for multiply-accumulate (MAC) units in convolutional neural network accelerators, particularly for power-constrained and fault-sensitive edge artificial intelligence applications.

Fatigue is a major safety concern in high-risk industries and can result from insufficient sleep, prolonged mental workload, and sustained physical exertion. While existing fatigue management approaches often focus on scheduling or generic interventions, they rarely provide personalized recommendations tailored to a worker’s current fatigue condition. To address this gap, a personalized fatigue mitigation recommendation system was designed to support fatigue risk management in offshore oil and gas extraction (OGE) operations. The system integrates research evidence and offshore expert consensus within a multi-criteria decision-making framework to generate individualized fatigue mitigation strategies based on workers’ fatigue profiles. The system considers four fatigue-related indicators: mental exhaustion, physical exertion, perceived sleepiness, and sleep loss. The recommendation system was applied to a real-world offshore fatigue dataset containing over 1,800 fatigue records collected from workers. Results demonstrated the feasibility of generating context-aware and personalized recommendations across a wide range of fatigue states.

Against the backdrop of digital media iteration and the expansion of China’s animation industry, aesthetic discourse surrounding female animated characters demonstrates differentiated structural features across production eras and evaluation contexts. Existing research is constrained by fragmented indicator systems, single-modality data, and a lack of standardized frameworks to support long-term cross-era quantitative comparison. To address these gaps, this study constructs a three-tier aesthetic evaluation framework consisting of Beauty of Image, Beauty of Impression, and Beauty of Idea, and proposes a dual-perspective quantitative workflow integrating large language model-based text mining, multimodal visual feature extraction, and the entropy-weighted TOPSIS method. Based on 72 representative Chinese animated works, 851,217 raw user comments, and 261 standardized character images, this study analyzes the distribution of aesthetic dimensions in both narrative-comment and pure-visual scenarios respectively, and validates the methodological reliability from three aspects: inter-annotator agreement, human–machine consistency, and test-retest stability. Quantitative results reveal that the two contexts present divergent aesthetic weight structures: identity-related dimensions exhibit the highest discriminative salience in narrative scenarios, while visual morphological attributes dominate in pure-visual settings. Across production eras, the discriminative salience of static morphological dimensions shows a steady upward trend, whereas the differentiating power of traditional cultural aesthetic dimensions declines gradually. High-frequency aesthetic vocabulary presents identity-oriented structural features in narrative contexts and form-and-style-oriented features in pure-visual scenarios respectively, with an overall evolutionary trend shifting toward visual detail orientation over time. This study empirically validates the effectiveness of the three-tier aesthetic framework and provides a standardized cross-era quantitative analytical paradigm for animation aesthetics research.

We evaluated a pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) psychiatry collaborative intervention designed to streamline mental and behavioral health (MBH) patient management and reduce emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS). Using electronic health record (EHR) data from 151,014 pediatric emergency department (PED) visits at a single urban PED in South Carolina between October 1, 2017, and November 30, 2023, we evaluated an intervention implemented on April 1, 2023 in which PEM physicians performed initial evaluations and promptly consulted psychiatry post-medical stabilization. Psychiatry then managed stable MBH patients through discharge or inpatient admission. An interrupted time series analysis with an ARIMA model assessed LOS among 8,791 pediatric MBH patients. The intervention system significantly reduced LOS by 81.3 min for MBH patients in the PED ( p < .001). Future research should replicate this intervention in diverse healthcare settings to assess generalizability and further refine strategies for improving care for pediatric MBH patients.
topics: Psychiatric care and mental health services

documents.abstract: Aircraft assembly requires repeatedly performing precision tasks at various heights and non-neutral positions. Prolonged exposure to non-neutral positions is a risk factor for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Traditional ergonomic assessments can support quantifying these risks, but are time consuming. Wearable motion sensing from Inertial Measurement Units (IMU) could support ergonomists quantifying postural exposure across work shifts. This study evaluated alignment between Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) shoulder and torso scores from a focus group of ergonomists and an IMU-based analysis using data collected from a worker performing assembly tasks. The proof-of-concept results suggest the proposed method is promising for identifying general postural exposure trends. Differences in expert perceptions and IMU-based analysis were observed, which could arise from the video format of the observations, including the point of view of the worker or the visual context. Further investigation should consider how to present IMU-based data to support ergonomist decision-making needs.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Overhead and awkward postures in assembly can shift muscular demands and accelerate localized fatigue. While electromyography (EMG) amplitude and frequency features are commonly used to assess fatigue, these features can be difficult to interpret independently. This proof-of-concept study applied the Joint Analysis of Spectrum and Amplitude (JASA) method to characterize biceps and triceps fatigue for select assembly-relevant tasks at three different heights using data from one experienced worker. For each task, slopes of root mean square (RMS) and median frequency were computed and mapped to JASA categories. Initial findings indicate fatigue patterns consistent with expectations associated with the task, height, and arm usage. Elevated height was more frequently associated with dominant triceps fatigue, with nominal and lowered heights more often associated with dominant biceps fatigue. The JASA method provides insight into disambiguating force increase/decrease from fatigue behavior and should be further evaluated to support ergonomic interventions in assembly work.

Automotive human factors knowledge is essential for early design decisions, yet relevant evidence is often dispersed across standards, design guidelines, regulatory resources, and research-based evidence. Designers must interpret these materials and translate them into actionable recommendations, which can limit timely use during conceptual design. This paper proposes a RAG–LLM-based method for automotive human factors design guidance. The method builds a task-oriented knowledge base from curated human factors materials, parses natural-language design inputs into structured intents, retrieves relevant evidence through semantic and terminology-based matching, and generates structured recommendations with source attribution. A prototype system demonstrated the workflow through a representative automotive HMI case, transforming an open-ended route-entry design task into evidence-grounded recommendations with inspectable sources. Preliminary user-oriented evaluation suggested usefulness for knowledge access, recommendation interpretation, and evidence review, indicating potential to support early-stage design reasoning.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from a specialist computing capability into a general-purpose technology used in customer service, marketing, finance, operations, information management, software development, and decision support. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in developing economies, these tools can create meaningful opportunities to improve productivity and service delivery. However, the conditions under which SMEs adopt AI are often very different from those of large firms and highly digitized economies. This paper develops a responsible AI adoption framework for SMEs in developing economies, with particular attention to Uganda, and grounds it in secondary data drawn from international and national reports and statistics. Global evidence shows that AI adoption has accelerated sharply, with 72% of surveyed organizations reporting AI use and 65% regularly using generative AI in at least one business function in 2024 (McKinsey & Company, 2024). In Uganda, however, internet penetration stood at 28.0% of the population and access to electricity at roughly 30% in recent measurements (DataReportal, 2025; International Energy Agency [IEA], 2023), while micro, small, and medium enterprises make up about 90% of private-sector production yet report only 35% technology adoption, with 53.4% of owners possessing neither a smartphone nor a computer (Ministry of Trade, Industry and Cooperatives [MTIC], 2024). This contrast is the empirical core of the paper: access alone does not explain or guarantee responsible AI adoption. The framework brings together the Technology-Organization- Environment (TOE) perspective, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), responsible AI governance principles, cybersecurity requirements, and the development context reflected in recent Ugandan policy materials. Six dimensions are proposed: technological readiness, organizational readiness, human capability, data readiness, environmental conditions, and responsible AI governance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of internet of things (IoT) applications has generated an urgent demand for efficient task scheduling mechanisms that feature low latency, scalability, and resource awareness. While fog computing can meet this demand by extending computing and storage resources to the vicinity of data sources, it still confronts four core challenges: resource heterogeneity, dynamic workloads, mobility, and security constraints. To address these issues, this study conducts a systematic review of intelligent task scheduling for fog-enabled IoT systems. It classifies the included eligible studies into five scheduling paradigms, and innovatively proposes a cross-domain framework that integrates three types of awareness, including priority awareness. The subsequent work of this study will sort out the core strengths and limitations of existing relevant methods. Finally, open challenges and emerging research directions, including edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning, blockchain-assisted scheduling, and hardware-accelerated implementations are discussed. The findings provide useful guidance for developing scalable, secure, and adaptive scheduling frameworks for next-generation fog-enabled IoT systems.

Independent mobility is essential to the daily lives of the growing population of people who are blind or visually impaired (PBVI). Although research on assistive mobility has expanded rapidly, limitations and challenges identified through empirical evaluations remain insufficiently synthesized. This scoping review examines 50 studies to investigate how PBVI wayfinding and navigation approaches have been empirically evaluated and to synthesize their reported shortcomings. In this review, wayfinding refers to route planning and environmental understanding, whereas navigation refers to real-time movement during travel. Four recurring themes emerged: device appearance, hardware and software performance, user interaction, and integration into daily life. We further identify critical questions that highlight gaps between existing approaches and user expectations. Based on these themes and cross-study implications, we develop a practical checklist that translates concerns from prior evaluations into actionable considerations for the future design and evaluation of assistive mobility technologies for PBVI.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Physical rehabilitation helps patients recover from injury and regain functional independence, but social and structural determinants of health, including living conditions, income, and transportation, can limit access to in-person care. Telerehabilitation addresses many of these barriers by enabling patients to complete therapy at home while supporting remote monitoring. However, the lack of direct supervision may reduce patient engagement, motivation, and adherence to prescribed exercises. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to develop adaptive, personalized rehabilitation systems that enhance the effectiveness of self-directed therapy. This scoping review examines current developments in AI-driven rehabilitation, focusing on the techniques used, evaluation methods employed, and user experiences reported across studies. By synthesizing recent research, the review identifies emerging trends, common challenges, and opportunities for future AI-enabled telerehabilitation systems that improve patient engagement and support long-term rehabilitation outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examined whether tactile detection reduces dual-task costs compared to visual detection when paired with a visual tracking task, and whether this advantage persists as temporal task load increases. Thirty-eight participants completed a visual tracking task and a detection task concurrently. The detection task was presented either visually or tactually, and temporal task load was manipulated by varying the stimulus presentation rate. Performance was analyzed using signal detection theory measures to determine whether differences between visual and tactile detection reflected changes in perceptual sensitivity, response bias, or both. Tactile detection produced smaller dual-task costs than visual detection across hit rate, false alarm rate, sensitivity, and response bias. Critically, tactile detection better preserved sensitivity under dual-task conditions, suggesting reduced perceptual competition with the visual tracking task. However, higher temporal load still degraded performance in the tactile condition. These findings support multimodal interface design while highlighting limits of modality diversification.

Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) image-to-video systems have lowered the technical threshold for presenting traditional cultural content in motion, while generated motion may alter characters, props, narrative relationships, craft features, composition, and symbols. This study implements a trustworthiness assessment workflow for traditional narrative images in architectural decoration, linking cultural evidence dossiers, sample-adapted prompts, computer-vision measurements, and blinded human coding. Eight source images were used to generate 120 videos under three prompt conditions, with five outputs per image–condition cell. Four coders assessed the videos, five experts reviewed the coding instrument, and two new coders independently assessed 48 videos. Primary deviation rates were 7.12%, 7.37%, and 9.07% for conditions A, B, and C, respectively, with no significant blocked difference after correction (Friedman χ2(2) = 1.400; Holm-adjusted p = 1.000). Mean item-level Krippendorff’s alpha was 0.250 across 14 estimable items; the independent-review composite ICC (A,1) was 0.402. Additional analyses examined coder sensitivity and the grouped generation structure. The original association involving inter-frame stability SSIM was not supported in within-image–condition comparisons (ρ = −0.052; permutation p = 0.610). An exploratory association was observed between source-image SSIM and human-coded deviations within these cells (ρ = −0.366; Holm-adjusted permutation p = 0.021). The study provides a documented procedure for comparing generated outputs and identifies limits in prompt effectiveness and the reproducibility of human judgments.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: As Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research continues to expand rapidly, synthesizing evidence on AD determinants across large scientific databases has become increasingly difficult at scale. This verification study compares human manual extraction with a Large Language Model (LLM) approach for identifying AD determinants from 10 systematic reviews retrieved from the Web of Science database. Two parallel extraction workflows were applied to the same source material. The human researcher identified 81 distinct determinants, whereas the LLM identified 74, with 44 human determinants and 41 LLM determinants overlapping across both approaches. While both methods showed strong alignment on well-established behavioral and lifestyle risk factors, the LLM frequently consolidated clinically distinct variables into broader umbrella categories, a pattern termed lossy consolidation. Although the LLM demonstrated major advantages in efficiency and quantitative evidence retrieval, the findings support hybrid evidence-synthesis workflows in which LLM extraction is combined with targeted human validation to preserve determinant-level clinical specificity.

Achieving Super Artificial Intelligence by 2028 A Three-Model Collaborative Architecture Based on a Memory System, Swarm Intelligence, and Real-Time Learning Author: William (Superintelligence Researcher and Architect) Abstract This paper proposes a system architecture for Super Artificial General Intelligence (SAGI) aimed at practical deployment by 2028. Driven by three core engines—the Physical Space Model (PSM), the Causal Reasoning Model (CRM), and the Decision & Verification Model (DVM)—and supported by three foundational infrastructure layers: the Memory System, Swarm Intelligence, and Real-Time Learning Intelligence, this architecture constructs a general-purpose intelligent agent capable of generating outputs with a near-100% probability of correctness. This paper details the design principles, collaborative mechanisms, and engineering implementation pathways for each module, providing a comprehensive technical blueprint for transitioning Super Artificial General Intelligence from theoretical concepts to real-world engineering deployment.

This paper proposes an adaptive stream processing architecture inspired by human cognitive constraints and bounded rationality to address information overload in high-throughput environments. Conventional stream processing architectures typically enforce uniform, full-context parsing, which leads to computational saturation, token explosions, and brittle exception-handling under extreme workloads. Rather than treating cognitive limitations as operational deficiencies, the proposed framework formalizes them as evolved resource-allocation strategies. The architecture introduces five functionally distinct processing modes: 1. Keyword Scanning (semantic compression) 2. Defensive Suppression (stability preservation) 3. Gestalt Peripheral Monitoring (macroscopic situation awareness) 4. Internal Loop Prioritization (internal resource reallocation) 5. Exploratory Sampling (search space diversity preservation via hash, random, or heuristic methods) Additionally, the framework integrates macro-level clustering with minority signal preservation to ensure simultaneous data compression and anomaly retention. By converting system saturation from a terminal exception into a controlled, adaptive mode transition, this methodology provides an engineering foundation for building resilient, context-aware information systems operating under persistent overload.

Despite the high safety risks in construction, on-site adoption of wearable technologies remains low, particularly in the Global South. This mixed-methods study examines construction stakeholders’ perceptions of WT adoption in Lebanon and the GCC, comparing findings with Global North benchmark studies. Data were collected via surveys and semi-structured interviews targeting 101 consulting and contracting professionals. Findings reveal high recognition of WT benefits, specifically for risk reduction ( M = 4 . 40 ) and hazard monitoring, primarily driven by safety-first motivations ( 67 . 3 % ). However, adoption remains low, with 63 . 4 % reporting minimal site usage ( < 25 % ). Primary barriers include privacy concerns ( 83 . 2 % ), implementation costs ( 77 . 2 % ), and trust or surveillance issues. Furthermore, adoption in the Middle East faces unique organizational and cultural challenges. Stronger regulatory frameworks and trust-building strategies are vital to accelerating practical WT integration.

Modern computer networks face a wide range of threats, including denial-of-service attacks, port scanning, brute-force attempts, botnet activity, and previously unseen malicious behaviour. Traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems can identify known patterns but may struggle when attack behaviour changes or has no existing signature. This paper reviews how Artificial Intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning can strengthen intrusion detection and network protection. It presents a conceptual layered framework combining network-flow collection, data preparation, AI-based classification, anomaly detection, explainable alerts, and human-supervised response. The paper discusses commonly used approaches such as decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, neural networks, and anomaly-detection models, alongside evaluation measures including precision, recall, F1-score, false-positive rate, and detection latency. Public benchmark datasets such as CICIDS2017 can support controlled evaluation, but their limitations mean that results must not be assumed to transfer directly to live networks. This is a literature-based conceptual study; it does not claim to have trained or experimentally validated a new model. The paper concludes that an effective AI-powered IDS requires reliable data, careful validation, privacy protection, analyst oversight, and continuous monitoring

Air pollution has emerged as a major environmental and public health concern, necessitating effective and continuous monitoring and accurate prediction of pollutant concentrations. The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML) offers promising solutions for real-time air quality monitoring, pollution forecasting, and proactive environmental management. This study examines the application of IoT-enabled sensor networks and AI-based predictive models in industrial and smart city environments through a secondary, desk-based review of three recent studies. The review analyses sensor-based data collection, machine learning algorithms, predictive performance, practical applications, and implementation challenges. The findings indicate that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks demonstrate strong predictive performance for time-dependent pollution data, while Random Forest models provide competitive results for specific pollutants, particularly particulate matter (PM2.5). The reviewed industrial application highlights the potential of AI-driven forecasting to support automated ventilation and early intervention, whereas the smart city application demonstrates the usefulness of predictive analytics in urban air quality management and evidence-based policymaking. Despite these benefits, challenges related to data quality, sensor calibration, scalability, system integration, and model interpretability remain significant. The study recommends improved sensor standardisation, hybrid modelling approaches, and Explainable AI techniques to enhance the reliability and practical adoption of these systems. It concludes that integrating IoT and AI can strengthen pollution control, protect public health, and support sustainable environmental management.

This article presents two corpora of English and Czech texts generated by large language models (LLMs). The motivation is to create a resource for comparing human-written texts with LLM-generated text linguistically. Emphasis was placed on ensuring these resources are multi-genre and diverse in terms of topics, authors, and text types, while maintaining comparability with existing human-created corpora. These generated corpora replicate reference human corpora: BE21 by Paul Baker, which is a modern version of the original Brown Corpus, and the Koditex corpus that also follows the Brown Corpus tradition but in Czech. The new corpora were generated using models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Alphabet, Meta, and DeepSeek, ranging from GPT-3 (davinci-002) to GPT−4.5, and are tagged according to the Universal Dependencies standard (i.e., they are tokenized, lemmatized, and morphologically and syntactically annotated). The subcorpus size varies by model used (the English part contains, on average, 864k tokens per model and 27 M tokens altogether; the Czech part contains on average 768k tokens per model, 21.5M tokens altogether). The corpora are freely available for download under the CC BY 4.0 license (the annotated data are under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license) and are also accessible through the search interface of the Czech National Corpus.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence in digital learning presents new opportunities to improve the quality of academic feedback, although its educational value may be associated with students’ motivational and self-regulatory characteristics. This study examined the relationships among AI-assisted feedback, digital motivation, self-regulated learning, and perceived academic performance of university students. Survey data were obtained from 337 students at two private universities in Makassar, Indonesia. The measurement model was evaluated through confirmatory factor analysis in LISREL 8.7 using the full eligible sample, whereas the structural model and mediation pathways were tested in AMOS 24 using 290 cases after multivariate outlier screening. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews with 15 purposively selected students to explain and contextualise the quantitative findings. The interview data were analysed using a theory-informed thematic analysis. Results showed that perceived AI-assisted feedback was positively associated with digital motivation and self-regulated learning. Digital motivation was positively associated with self-regulated learning, while both digital motivation and self-regulated learning were positively associated with perceived academic performance. Indirect associations were significant through digital motivation, through self-regulated learning, and sequentially through digital motivation and self-regulated learning. Qualitative findings showed that students valued AI-assisted feedback for error identification, revision guidance, progress monitoring, and reflection. However, one participant reported that some suggestions were overly general and required lecturer validation. The results indicate that AI-assisted feedback might be more educationally valuable when accompanied by critical feedback evaluation, reflective revision, and support for self-regulated learning. Because the design was cross-sectional and the outcome was self-reported, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects.

Phishing websites are a major cybersecurity threat because they imitate legitimate websites to deceive users into revealing sensitive information, including passwords, financial details, and personal data. Traditional phishing detection techniques, such as blocklists and manually defined rules, may fail to identify newly created or rapidly modified malicious websites. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer a data-driven approach to identifying suspicious websites through the analysis of URL characteristics and other website-related features. This paper presents an empirical evaluation framework for comparing machine learning algorithms for phishing website detection. The proposed study uses the publicly available UCI Phishing Websites dataset, which contains 11,055 instances and 30 predictive features. Four supervised learning algorithms—Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine—are selected for comparative evaluation. The methodology incorporates data preprocessing, stratified training and testing, cross-validation, feature-importance analysis, and multiple performance metrics, including precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Existing research indicates that ensemble learning methods, particularly Random Forest, are promising for this classification task; however, performance depends on dataset characteristics and experimental design. Since no new model execution was conducted for this manuscript, numerical experimental results are not claimed. The proposed framework supports reproducible evaluation and highlights the importance of temporal validation, interpretable predictions, and real-world testing in developing reliable phishing detection systems.

The National Education Policy 2020 commits India to a digitally delivered, openly licensed education system built on repositories such as DIKSHA and SWAYAM, whose architecture presupposes that someone - a teacher, an institution, an author - holds clear, licensable rights in the content those repositories host. That presupposition is now in tension with a faster-moving development: generative artificial intelligence tools are already drafting, translating, and illustrating educational content across Indian schools and universities, often without any settled answer to whether the resulting material is protected by copyright at all, and if so, whose. This chapter examines that tension through India's still-unsettled copyright law on artificial intelligence, read specifically through the lens of educational content rather than commercial creative industries. It traces the Copyright Act 1957's computer-generated-work provision, Section 2(d)(vi), against the Copyright Office's 2020 registration and subsequent withdrawal notice concerning the RAGHAV-assisted work Suryast; the Delhi High Court's July 2026 interim ruling in ANI Media v. OpenAI on fair dealing under Section 52; and the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade's December 2025 working paper proposing mandatory blanket licensing for AI training data, which addresses only the input side of the problem and leaves authorship of AI-generated output for a still-unpublished Part II. Comparing India's position with the United States' human-authorship doctrine, the European Union's transparency-based regime under the AI Act, and China's mandatory content-labelling rules, the chapter argues that Indian education sits at the intersection of two distinct regulatory gaps - an unresolved general question of AI authorship, and an education policy architecture that has not yet asked that question in sector-specific terms - and that closing the second gap need not wait on the first.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming education, employment, healthcare, mobility, communication, and public services, yet its benefits are not equally accessible to neurodivergent individuals, particularly in the Global South. Conventional digital inclusion approachesemphasizetechnologicalaccesswhileoftenoverlookingcognitiveaccessibility,sensory differences,communicationpreferences,anddiverse interactionpatterns.This manuscriptproposes an integrated framework for AI-enabled neuro-inclusion that places neurodiversity, accessibility, human autonomy, transparency, privacy, and participatory design at the center of responsible AI development. The framework connects technology design with institutional governance and measurable inclusion outcomes across education, employment, public services, and digital participation. It examines neuro-inclusive software development, AI-assisted sensory accessibility assessment, and accreditation-based standards as implementation mechanisms. Using India and the wider Global South as application contexts, the manuscript positions neuro-inclusion as a component of responsible innovation, equitable digital transformation, and sustainable human development
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: An emergency operations center (EOC) is the central hub of activity during a coordinated disaster response. The layout of an EOC must be intuitive, conducive to communication, and free of distractions. We use a mix of objective and subjective measures to inform layout decisions that aid interagency coordination, build effective transactive memory systems, and create resilient teams. We observed an annual drill at an EOC involving 65 individuals. Subjective responses indicate that the physical arrangement of the EOC may be of little importance, given participants’ willingness to move. Audio analysis reveals high degrees of centrality, despite uneven speaking shares, suggesting all speakers within EOC subgroups contribute to group-work. Video analysis exhibits strong temporal consistency, though future work is needed to improve detection confidence. Results demonstrate the plausibility of deploying multimodal methodologies to an EOC, as we find moderate success with video-based metrics and sensitivity to intra-team dynamics with audio recordings.

India's chemical sector, worth an estimated $300 billion and contributing roughly seven per cent of national GDP, sits at an unusual junction: it is simultaneously one of the country's most consequential engines of economic growth and one of its least regulated sources of solvent waste, energy-intensive processing, and hazardous by-product generation, with no REACH-equivalent statutory framework yet in place to govern any of it. Globally, artificial intelligence is already reshaping the discipline that promises to resolve that tension - green chemistry - through machine-learning models that predict reaction yield and selectivity before a single flask is used, generative platforms that screen thousands of candidate solvents and catalysts in silico, and autonomous laboratories that compress materials-discovery timelines historically measured in decades into a year or two. This chapter examines what that convergence means specifically for India's higher-education system as it implements the National Education Policy 2020, treating artificial intelligence and green chemistry not as two separate curricular add-ons but as a single, mutually reinforcing case study in the multidisciplinary, research-intensive, skill-based science education NEP 2020 calls for. Drawing on the recent international literature on AI-enabled green chemistry, India's still-forming research-financing architecture under the Anusandhan National Research Foundation and the IndiaAI Mission, the existing UGC-mandated NEP chemistry curriculum, and systematic-review evidence on how NEP 2020's research and multidisciplinary provisions have actually been implemented on the ground, the chapter argues that India possesses unusually strong raw material for this convergence - a large chemical industry, a credible national-laboratory research base, and a curricular mandate for interdisciplinary, skill-based learning - but has not yet built the pedagogical, regulatory, or funding scaffolding needed to connect them, and that closing this gap is now a distinct and separable task from either the AI-education debate or the green-chemistry-regulation debate considered alone.

India's digital payments ecosystem processed over nineteen billion transactions in a single month of 2025, a volume that has made artificial intelligence not an optional enhancement to fraud control but its practical precondition: no team of human analysts can review transactions at the speed a fraudulent transfer takes to clear. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence is being deployed to detect and prevent fraud across India's Unified Payments Interface and wider digital payments infrastructure, and how India's regulatory architecture - the Reserve Bank of India's Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, the forthcoming Digital Payments Intelligence Platform, the National Payments Corporation of India's real-time fraud-scoring infrastructure, and the Reserve Bank's 2025 Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence - is attempting to govern that deployment. Drawing on the Reserve Bank's FY2024-25 fraud data, parliamentary disclosures on Unified Payments Interface fraud, and the still-unsettled statistics surrounding so-called digital arrest scams, the chapter documents both the scale of algorithmically mediated fraud and the significant inconsistencies across India's own reporting systems for measuring it. It reviews the peer-reviewed literature on machine learning and deep learning approaches to payment fraud detection, situates India's institutional response within that literature, and argues that the country's fraud-control architecture has matured faster on the detection side than on the harder, still-unresolved question of how aggressive algorithmic fraud prevention is to be reconciled with the financial-inclusion mandate that drove UPI's design in the first place.

Scams targeting older adults increasingly combine social engineering with generative technology such as voice cloning, video deepfakes and text produced by large language models (LLMs). Adults aged 60 and over reported losses of USD 7.7 billion to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025, 59% more than in 2024. This review, supported by a documented search of four databases (2019–2026), examines how such scams are structured, why older adults are susceptible, and how artificial intelligence (AI) can detect or mitigate them. Of 992 screened records, 60 studies met the eligibility criteria, and three more were identified through citation chasing. Most evaluations with older users measured knowledge, confidence or intentions after an educational intervention; where detection performance or real-world exposure was measured, results were mixed and often null. None of the included studies evaluated an AI-based scam-detection system with older users in a field setting, and the only study testing audio-deepfake detectors on older speakers found that detectors trained on standard benchmarks roughly doubled their error rate. We propose a six-layer conceptual framework, not yet validated, for engineering elder-scam protection as a socio-technical system, and identify age-diverse evaluation, field trials of real-time assistance, privacy preservation and trust calibration as the principal open challenges.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping Accounting Information Systems (AIS) by allowing firms to automate mundane accounting tasks, contribute to managerial decision-making, enhance auditing processes, and increase the accuracy of financial reporting. Traditional AIS are mostly created on the basis of specified rules, human data processing and traditional internal controls. This can restrict their capacity to review vast quantities of sophisticated financial data in a timely manner. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies including machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation and predictive analytics offer fresh answers to these limitations. This paper critically reviews the role of AI in AIS. It’s about the effect of artificial intelligence on the accuracy of financial statements, the effectiveness of auditing, fraud detection and the development of strategic options. It is a conceptual approach to research that involves a comprehensive review of relevant literacy and decision-making frameworks and professional standards. The paper said artificial intelligence can enhance transaction classification, identify financial anomalies, speed audit data analysis and provide real-time financial insights. However, some of these benefits depend on cybersecurity, governance, expert monitoring, data integrity and system stability. The essay also discusses other issues such as algorithmic bias, explanations, implementation costs, privacy problems, and the ever-expanding skill set that accountants must acquire. Therefore, AI should not replace the professional judgment of accountants, but rather used as a tool to assist them in making those decisions. The report concludes with a call for a shared governance model, a call for technical innovation along with human accountability, ethical safeguards and ongoing oversight. The results of this research are useful for organizations who want to enhance their accounting procedures in a more advanced and data driven commercial environment.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in the fields of medicine and ophthalmology. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and convolutional neural networks have significantly improved cataract detection and grading, intraocular lens power calculations, surgical decision‐making, risk prediction and patient education. Intraoperative AI‐assisted surgical phase recognition, workflow analysis, real‐time guidance, robotic technologies and femtosecond laser integration can improve surgical precision, efficiency and safety. AI has shown promise in predicting visual outcomes, detecting postoperative complications and facilitating telemedicine follow‐up. Though challenges with AI include transparency, data diversity, regulatory oversight and clinical validation, continued advances are expected to further personalise cataract surgery, support clinical decision‐making, optimise surgical performance and improve patient outcomes. This narrative summarises the current and emerging applications of AI in preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative management of cataracts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming disaster risk reduction and management by enhancing prediction, preparedness, response, and recovery. Leveraging techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, AI can analyse diverse datasets, including satellite imagery, sensor networks, social media, and historical disaster records, to improve early warning systems and risk assessments. AI applications range from predictive modelling of floods, earthquakes, landslides, and tropical cyclones to real-time damage assessment using computer vision and drones, and optimised emergency response planning. Additionally, AI supports post-disaster reconstruction and long-term recovery through economic modelling, infrastructure planning, and psychological support. Despite these benefits, challenges such as data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy concerns, and infrastructure requirements must be addressed to ensure equitable and effective deployment. Incorporating ethical frameworks, community engagement, and transparency is essential for maximising AI’s potential in building resilient communities and mitigating the social, economical, and environmental impacts of disasters.

This study aims to conduct a comprehensive bibliometric and thematic mapping analysis of global research at the intersection of endometriosis and artificial intelligence (AI). Using bibliographic data indexed in the Scopus database between 2001 and 2026, the study investigates temporal publication trends, citation patterns, prolific countries, collaborative networks, prominent journals, institutions, key authors, AI methodological distributions (e.g., machine learning, deep learning), and specific thematic clinical domains (e.g., diagnostic imaging, biomarkers/omics).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering Indian classrooms and campuses from two directions at once: as asubject to be taught, through the Central Board of Secondary Education's AI curriculum and the AllIndia Council for Technical Education's 2025 "Year of AI," and as a tool already in use, throughgenerative systems that more than eight lakh school students and an unmeasured but clearly largeshare of higher-education students have adopted faster than any institutional framework has been builtto govern them. This chapter examines both movements together, treating "opportunities" and"challenges" not as a balanced-scorecard exercise but as two faces of the same underlying fact: Indiais scaling AI-in-education faster at the level of enrolment and policy announcement than at the level ofinfrastructure, teacher preparedness, or regulatory clarity. Drawing on national curriculum andregulatory documents, a 2025 preparedness-framework policy brief, Lok Sabha enrolment data,documented cases of both student and faculty misuse, and UNESCO's 2024 AI competencyframeworks, the chapter finds a now-familiar pattern from across this volume repeated at theclassroom level: sixty-six per cent of Indian schools still lack functional internet access even as AIcurricula are mandated from Class 3 onward, and Indian students have made ChatGPT a daily studytool at a scale global usage figures suggest is unmatched, while the Union Grants Commission has yetto issue a binding, numeric standard for what counts as impermissible AI use in academic work. Thechapter argues that the opportunities this technology genuinely offers - personalised and multilinguallearning, teacher-workload relief, and expanded access for learners with disabilities - are real andevidenced, but that realising them at the scale NEP 2020 envisions depends on closing exactly theinfrastructure, training, and regulatory gaps the same evidence base documents.

documents.abstract: This student literature review explores the applications and challenges of artificial intelligence in space exploration. It examines AI-assisted planetary rover navigation, autonomous scientific target selection, exoplanet discovery, Earth-observing satellites, onboard data processing, and space debris monitoring. The paper also discusses technical limitations, including radiation effects, computational constraints, model reliability, and safety verification.

Artificial intelligence recommendation systems now shape how consumers discover and evaluate products online, yet research on their influence on purchase intention remains scattered across theories, contexts and methods. This study presents a systematic literature review following the Scientific Procedures and Rationales for Systematic Literature Reviews protocol. A Scopus search covering January 2015 to March 2026 returned 1,779 records, which were screened to 397 and then to a final sample of 112 peer reviewed journal articles. The sample was analysed through bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer and Biblioshiny, including keyword co-occurrence, thematic maps and thematic evolution, and through the Theory, Context, Characteristics and Methodology (TCCM) framework. The literature draws mainly on the Stimulus Organism Response model, the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and trust theory. Most studies report that personalization, recommendation quality, transparency, explainability and trust are associated with stronger purchase intention, while privacy concerns, perceived manipulation and algorithmic bias weaken acceptance. Research is concentrated in e commerce and technologically advanced markets and relies mainly on cross sectional surveys and structural equation modelling. The review identifies gaps in explainable and ethical AI, consumer resistance, emerging market and cross-cultural evidence, and longitudinal and experimental designs, and it proposes a structured agenda for future research. Findings concern intentions rather than observed purchasing and reflect a single database.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including chatbots, generative language models, and AI-enabled simulation, are increasingly used in nursing programs, yet it remains unclear whether improvements in knowledge translate into observed clinical performance. This systematic review and meta-analysis, reported in line with PRISMA 2020, synthesised comparative studies of AI-supported learning among nursing students, treating knowledge, practical performance, and reasoning outcomes separately. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception, and screening and data extraction were conducted independently by the primary author and verified by a research colleague. Risk of bias was appraised with ROBINS-I (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions) for non-randomized studies and RoB 2 (Risk of Bias tool version 2) for randomized trials, and standardized mean differences were to be pooled with random-effects models where studies reported comparable outcomes. Not all eligible studies could be obtained in full text, so the synthesis was restricted to those that were accessible. These were non-randomized, single-site studies, most of them at serious risk of bias. Findings for knowledge were inconsistent: one study showed a very large benefit for a purpose-built chatbot, another showed no clear difference, and the disagreement was too great to support a meaningful pooled estimate. None of the analyzed studies assessed observed clinical performance, and one study of a general-purpose language model reported poorer rubric-scored work than textbook-based learning. Self-reported reasoning outcomes were uncertain and rested on unblinded self-rating. Current evidence does not show that AI-supported learning improves clinical performance among nursing students, and inaccessible full texts and the methodological weaknesses of the primary studies limit the conclusions. Future research should use randomized designs, validated observed-performance measures with blinded assessment, and active comparators matched for time and content.
