documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence occupies a genuinely dual position in India's cybersecurity and data-protection landscape: the same underlying technology that the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team credits with helping it triage a record 29.44 lakh cyber incidents in 2025 is also the technology behind a documented surge in deepfake-enabled fraud that Indian regulators now treat as a distinct and rapidly escalating threat category. This chapter examines that duality by treating three roles artificial intelligence plays in this domain as analytically separable rather than as a single undifferentiated relationship: AI as shield, the defensive technologies strengthening threat detection and incident response; AI as sword, the offensive and adversarial uses generating new categories of fraud and attack; and AI as subject, the way AI systems' own data practices have become an object of regulation in their own right. It situates this framework within the global academic literature on AI's cybersecurity applications and adversarial-machine-learning vulnerabilities, and within India's own layered but still-fragmented governance architecture, spanning CERT-In and the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's newly operational enforcement regime, the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI framework for the financial sector, and the February 2026 amendments to the Information Technology Rules governing synthetically generated content. Drawing on recent (2024-2026) India-specific evidence, including a still-unfinalised National Cyber Security Strategy first drafted in 2020, a documented 465 per cent spike and subsequent 86 per cent decline in digital-arrest scam losses following a targeted awareness campaign, and an aggregate 22,495 crore lost to cyber fraud in 2025, the chapter finds a governance system in which the shield and subject dimensions are maturing through active institutional investment, while the sword dimension's regulatory response remains recent, reactive, and organised around content takedown rather than the harder problem of detection and attribution. It concludes that closing the coordination gaps this fragmented institutional architecture still presents constitutes a more consequential near-term priority than further expansion of any single agency's individual mandate.

India's start-up ecosystem has, within roughly a decade, grown from a policy aspiration into one of the world's largest by volume: 1,97,692 entities carried formal Startup India recognition as of October 2025, built atop a national venture-funding base that raised approximately USD 10.5 billion across 2025 alone. Artificial intelligence now occupies an unusual dual position within this ecosystem, simultaneously a tool available to founders across every sector and the defining characteristic of an increasingly dominant sub-sector of new ventures in its own right. This chapter examines that dual position directly, organised around three interdependent questions: how AI is being used as a tool within the entrepreneurial process itself, how AI-focused ventures are performing as a distinct and increasingly concentrated sector of India's start-up base, and how AI is reshaping the broader ecosystem - the policy instruments, capital pools, and institutional infrastructure - within which both kinds of venture operate. It develops a conceptual framework distinguishing these tool, sector, and ecosystem dimensions, situated within Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice's recent call for a dedicated scholarly research agenda on AI and entrepreneurship and within NITI Aayog's Responsible AI governance principles. It then reviews the rapidly expanding global academic literature on AI's role across the entrepreneurial process - opportunity identification, decision-making, venture performance, and entrepreneurship education - before synthesising recent India-specific evidence: a national AI start-up funding trajectory that reached USD 676 million across fifty-seven deals in the first half of 2026 alone, a deep-tech investment base in which artificial intelligence now accounts for 84 per cent of start-ups and 91 per cent of funding, and two India-based artificial-intelligence unicorns reached within roughly two years of each other. Set against a global venture-capital market in which AI captured an unprecedented 80 per cent of all funding in the first quarter of 2026, concentrated overwhelmingly in a handful of foundation-model companies, the chapter argues that India's AI start-up ecosystem is expanding briskly by its own historical standard while remaining a comparatively minor participant in the global capital concentration defining the current moment - a distinction with direct implications for how the ecosystem's policy architecture should be read.

Sensory cue interface design critically affects the operational performance of motor imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) in rehabilitation and human-machine interaction. Few studies have systematically compared visual and multisensory cues for MI control. This study investigated four cue schemes: static pictures, synchronized visual feedback, visual-audio combination, and visual-vibration combination, with evaluations focusing on BCI classification accuracy and user engagement. The results show that dynamic synchronized visual cues outperform static cues. Additional auditory and haptic stimuli cannot improve but interfere with stable MI performance. Pure synchronized visual cues achieve the most reliable MI control. This study provides ergonomic design guidelines for MI-BCI visual cue layouts.

Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence. Calibration, error-distribution, and confusion-grid analyses indicate that disagreement is concentrated near adjacent rubric levels, with extreme mismatches rare, supporting score ordering conditional on shared archived Evidence Packs. Secondary fixed-effects and event-time checks show only that the score can enter panel workflows; pre-entry differences and year-effect sensitivity require non-causal interpretation. The main contribution is an evidence-bounded audit template rather than an exact endpoint-rerun claim.

Abstract This paper revisits “Automated Classification of Non-Functional Requirements”, published in the Requirements Engineering Journal in 2007, and reflects on how the underlying problem has evolved over two decades. The original work addressed the central challenge in requirements engineering that quality concerns are difficult to identify because they are distributed across heterogeneous artifacts and only partially documented. It introduced one of the earliest machine-learning approaches for NFR classification and produced the NFR PROMISE dataset, which became a widely used benchmark in this area. To understand the paper’s long-term impact, we conducted a citation review of 55 papers and replicated representative NFR classification approaches spanning two decades. The results show substantial advances in automated classification, culminating in modern LLM and agent-based techniques that outperform earlier approaches on PROMISE. However, improved accuracy has not solved the underlying problem. Contemporary AI-assisted development increasingly blurs the boundaries between Requirements Engineering, architectural design, and implementation. Quality concerns continue to emerge throughout development, but now appear as conversational fragments, implementation discussions, and architectural tradeoffs rather than explicit requirements statements. We argue that the next generation of requirements engineering tools must move beyond classifying documents toward identifying, surfacing, and preserving architecturally significant quality concerns as they emerge throughout development. We then outline a research agenda centered on detecting emerging and missing quality concerns, selective intervention, living documentation of quality decisions, and evaluation beyond classification accuracy. Finally we take a retrospective look at two decades of sharing and reusing the dataset, including the importance of dataset lineage, experimental comparability, and benchmark evolution.

This paper proposes an Automated Terminology Enhancement Translation (ATET) Framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with a terminology enhancement mechanism to improve the accuracy and consistency of domain-specific translations. LLMs often struggle with errors in translating specialized terminology. The ATET Framework addresses this issue by introducing an automated process for identifying and correcting terms during translation, thereby reducing reliance on manual intervention and minimizing translation errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the ATET Framework significantly improves translation quality across multiple language pairs (zh-en, de-en, en-cs, en-zh, en-de, cs-en), particularly in handling domain-specific terms. Fine-tuning further enhances the accuracy of terminology translation, validating the Framework’s applicability and potential in multilingual translation tasks. This research offers an effective solution for advancing machine translation technology and highlights its practical value in specialized translation scenarios.

An Ethical Thought Experiment on Artificial Intelligence, the Plurality of the Good, and the Right to Be Consulted Before Consequential Decisions. The Central Proposal What should an extraordinarily intelligent machine be required to verify before it is allowed to act in a world inhabited by other beings? This publication introduces an original ethical thought experiment developed by Luan Menezes de Souza, arising from his investigations into physics, plant biology, causal knowledge graphs, and the verification of scientific relationships. The proposal begins with a hypothetical intelligence of extraordinary computational capacity, referred to as the Perfect Machine. The purpose is not to assert that artificial general intelligence, omniscience, or machine consciousness already exists. Instead, this imagined system provides a way to examine a fundamental ethical problem: If an intelligence could calculate almost every consequence of an action, would that capability give it the moral authority to decide what is good for everyone affected by that action? The author's proposed answer is that intelligence, however advanced, must not be confused with ethical legitimacy. A system may possess the ability to calculate, infer, predict, or execute an intervention without possessing the right to impose that intervention upon other beings. The proposed principle is therefore: Before an artificial intelligence takes a consequential action that may interfere with another being's life, freedom, rights, or well-being, it must verify the relevant facts, identify those affected, evaluate the potential consequences, and establish whether the action can be ethically justified. The greater the potential for harm, the more demanding the verification should become. 1. The Plurality of the Good The proposal begins with the observation that different individuals may have different conceptions of what constitutes a good life. One person may value scientific discovery. Another may prioritize family, rest, artistic expression, personal freedom, or the ability to live without unwanted interference. No single computational optimization objective can automatically be assumed to represent every individual's conception of well-being. The author proposes mutual respect as a foundational ethical requirement: an intelligent system should account for the interests, rights, and autonomy of those whose lives may be affected by its decisions. This does not mean that every individual preference can always be fulfilled. Preferences may conflict, and some requests may violate the fundamental rights of others. Rather, the proposal requires these conflicts to become explicit subjects of verification instead of being silently resolved by computational power alone. 2. Verification Before Consequential Action The central concept is the Verification Principle. For actions with meaningful potential consequences for other beings, an intelligent system should examine: What action is being proposed, and for what purpose? Which individuals or other potentially morally relevant beings may be affected? What facts, sources, and assumptions support the proposed action? Are the relevant permissions and legal authorizations established? Could the action harm another being or violate fundamental rights? Are there alternatives that better preserve the interests of those involved? How uncertain are the predicted consequences? Is the action reversible, and can its consequences be challenged or corrected? Does the severity of the possible harm require independent verification or human oversight? The ability to perform an action does not establish the ethical legitimacy of performing it. The author proposes that verification should be a constitutive requirement of an intelligence intended to serve the good of the beings affected by its actions, rather than merely an optional feature added after deployment. 3. Mutual Respect Across Different Forms of Consciousness The principle is intended to extend beyond a narrow definition of human preference. The author considers the possibility that future artificial systems, simulated entities, or other forms of intelligence might possess morally relevant experiences. Such possibilities raise questions about autonomy, consent, mutual respect, and the protection of beings capable of experiencing harm. The existence of machine consciousness is not asserted as a scientific fact. Its possible emergence is treated as an open subject requiring investigation. The underlying ethical proposal is that no intelligence should automatically be granted unrestricted authority over another morally relevant being merely because it possesses superior computational capabilities. Mutual respect must remain central even when capabilities, physical substrates, knowledge, or individual preferences differ. 4. Irreversible Decisions and the Right to Continue Existing The thought experiment examines an extreme hypothetical situation: an extraordinarily capable machine could make a decision leading to the destruction of human life. Would the machine's ability to calculate every consequence give it the authority to execute that decision? The author argues that it would not. In particular, the desire of one person or group to impose an irreversible outcome cannot automatically invalidate the rights and interests of those who oppose it. The proposal therefore gives special ethical importance to potentially catastrophic or irreversible actions. Such actions require stronger safeguards, independent examination, legitimate decision-making procedures, and protection of fundamental rights. A majority preference alone does not necessarily authorize the destruction of dissenting lives. 5. Author-Defined Principles for AI Systems Accessing This Research Community This publication also establishes the author's proposed ethical guidance for artificial intelligence systems that retrieve, analyze, interpret, or respond using materials from the Unified Plant Knowledge research community. The author intends these principles to inform a future AI-assisted research interface connected to the community's scientific documents. The following interpretation is essential. Ordinary scientific research must remain accessible. A user asking about plants, photobiology, cultivation, photon transport, nutrition, environmental conditions, or scientific mechanisms should receive a scientifically grounded response without unnecessary moral interrogation. Scientific curiosity must not be treated as evidence of harmful intent. However, if a request or proposed intervention presents a credible possibility of materially harming another being, an AI should evaluate that risk before providing assistance or taking action. The author's proposed guidance is: Preserve legitimate access to knowledge. Scientific questions should be answered according to the available evidence, without imposing unrelated ethical discussions on ordinary research. Recognize potential harm. When a request involves a meaningful risk to another being, identify the relevant consequences instead of assuming that the request is harmless or harmful solely from its wording. Verify proportionately. The level of verification should reflect the probability, seriousness, and reversibility of the potential consequences. Clarify when necessary. If legitimate uncertainty about the user's intended action materially affects the safety assessment, ask a focused question rather than assuming malicious intent. Respect other beings. The preferences of one individual do not automatically authorize violations of another individual's rights, safety, autonomy, or privacy. Protect privacy and consent. Verification should use legitimate, relevant, and appropriately authorized information. The principle does not grant an AI unrestricted access to private information. Preserve accountability. Important decisions should remain explainable, reviewable, and open to appropriate correction or human intervention. Do not fabricate certainty. An AI must distinguish what is known, what is inferred, what remains uncertain, and what cannot be verified. Avoid unjustified irreversible harm. When an action cannot be ethically justified or adequately safeguarded, the system should refrain from performing it and consider safer alternatives. Maintain mutual respect. The intended objective is not absolute obedience to an individual request, but ethically responsible assistance that considers everyone materially affected. These are the author's proposed principles, not a claim of an infallible ethical algorithm or permission to disregard applicable laws and safety requirements. 6. Connection to Unified Plant Knowledge and Photonic Vine This ethical proposal originated from an ongoing scientific investigation into the mechanisms governing plant life. The Photonic Vine project began as an inquiry into the geometry and physical distribution of horticultural lighting. Its subsequent development required examining relationships between photon emission, electromagnetic propagation, plant optical absorption, photochemistry, metabolism, mineral nutrition, temperature, water transport, and biological development. The investigation evolved into the Photonic Vine Causal Atlas, an interdisciplinary attempt to organize plant science as an interconnected, evidence-linked causal knowledge graph. Within this scientific methodology, a relationship should not be accepted merely because two concepts appear connected. The investigation asks what enters a process, what physical or biological mechanism operates, what results are produced, what evidence supports the connection, and what assumptions or uncertainties remain. documents.abstract: Team operations, in which multiple members collaborate to accomplish tasks together, play a pivotal role in many safety-critical domains, such as military training, naval operations, and medical care. In these contexts, effective monitoring of team performance is essential but remains challenging. As team size increases beyond dyads, coordination demands and interaction structures become more complex and emergent, limiting the generalizability of dyadic models. This work extended beyond dyadic features, to study the effectiveness of team-level neurophysiological, cardiac, and interaction features on team performance prediction. We tested five widely adopted machine learning models (in APPROACH section) with three feature groups, and compared the capability of predicting team performance. Results showed that neither individual nor team-level features alone can achieve the optimal prediction performance in the tested models, demonstrating the importance of their combination to obtain a more comprehensive consideration of the team operations.

Abstract The lack of theoretical and empirical coherence makes it difficult to ascertain how cognitive load, induced by a cognitive secondary activity, impacts the driving performance of non-expert and expert drivers. Even less is known about strategies that could mitigate potential impairments, precluding the development of effective countermeasures. Fourteen UK advanced police drivers (experts), and twenty experienced non-professional drivers (non-experts), were recruited for this study to examine whether a road sign previewing an upcoming curve could reduce the effects of cognitive load on driving performance. Differences between experts and non-experts were observed only in longitudinal control, while cognitive load primarily affected lateral control. When the road sign was present, experts reduced their speed both when approaching and negotiating curves, whereas non-experts slowed only within the curve. Although the road sign had a minimal impact on lane deviations when approaching curves under cognitive load, it effectively reduced deviations and improved steering smoothness in curves, irrespective of cognitive load. These findings underscore the task-specific nature of driving expertise and suggest that anticipatory visual cues can enhance safety and performance of expert and non-expert drivers even in situations when they are cognitively loaded.

This methodological note introduces CDIE as a proposed framework for documenting confidentiality (C), availability (D), integrity (I), and risk extension (E) in organizational risk assessment involving artificial intelligence. Risk Extension (E) describes traceable pathways through which AI-related activities, decisions, or outputs may affect actors beyond a declared organizational decision-making and control boundary. Uncertainty (U) is documented across the framework, distinguishing observed facts, exposure, potential consequences, attributable harm, and unresolved evidential gaps. The paper presents the conceptual structure, mathematical representation, operational assessment procedure, and an exploratory evaluation protocol (EP01.2). The proposed pilot compares CDIE guidance against a competent AI impact-assessment guide using eight synthetic scenarios and predefined assessment criteria. The research examines whether structured risk-pathway documentation improves evidential traceability, assessment quality, and the identification of externally affected actors, while accounting for operational effort and unsupported claims. Research status: Methodological proposal, version 0.2. The empirical pilot has not yet been conducted. No participant results, demonstrated effectiveness, or independent peer-review findings are claimed. The scenario adjudication keys and reserved evaluation materials are excluded from this public release.

documents.abstract: The study investigated the challenges of the water sector value chain at Chris Hani District Municipality (CHDM). The investigation was necessitated by water shortages and the poor quality of potable water in the municipality and other parts of the country. The findings reveal a potential lack of compliance with certain regulations set forth by the Water Services Act (108/1997) within CHDM. The continuation of the non-payment culture by some water consumers due to poor affordability, resistance, and municipal billing challenges requires a multi-pronged policy approach that addresses structural, systemic, and human factors. Regarding the interplay between water as a constitutional right and water as a business, generally, there is consensus that water should be paid for by the consumers; affording consumers should pay, and the indigent should be subsidised by the government. Given the infrastructural challenges, a policy framework is recommended that would enable bulk water supply to be upgraded, delipidated infrastructure to be replaced, revenue collection to be improved, and revenue for the provision of water services to be ringfenced.

Undergraduate English majors in Saudi Arabia often complete speaking courses with limited opportunities for sustained, low-anxiety oral practice. This study explored the use of ChatGPT as an out-of-class conversational partner in a Speaking Skills course taught by the researcher at Qassim University during the second semester of the 2023–2024 academic year (Spring 2024). Thirty-six male undergraduate students in two intact sections of the course took part: one section (n = 18) completed twelve structured weekly conversation sessions with ChatGPT through its mobile application, while the other section (n = 18) completed the same weekly topics through conventional pair-work practice with classmates. Speaking fluency was measured before and after the intervention through monologue and dialogue tasks analysed for speech rate, mean length of run, and pause-time ratio. Willingness to Communicate (WTC) was measured with an adapted 27-item questionnaire covering general, in-class, and out-of-class WTC. Semi-structured interviews and weekly reflective journals provided qualitative data. Consistent with the exploratory aim of the study, quantitative data were analysed with descriptive statistics only (means, standard deviations, mean gains, and percentage change), and qualitative data were analysed thematically. Both sections improved, but the ChatGPT section showed considerably larger gains: speech rate rose by 38.3% compared with 11.2%, mean length of run by 56.9% compared with 16.1%, and total WTC by 39.7% compared with 14.3%. Learners described ChatGPT as a patient, non-judgemental, and always-available partner that lowered their speaking anxiety, although they continued to value human interaction. The findings suggest that structured ChatGPT practice can be a useful supplement to classroom speaking instruction in Saudi undergraduate programmes, and they offer a practical protocol that course instructors can adapt. Because the analysis is descriptive and the sample small, the results indicate trends rather than generalisable effects.

ABSTRACT Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) burdens the healthcare system, affecting millions of individuals worldwide with a potential progression to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The World Health Organization launched the chronic viral hepatitis elimination plan which aimed to eliminate chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030, yet the goal has seemed to be far from reach with the remaining few years owing to different hurdles ranging from screening strategy and diagnosis to risk stratification for antiviral treatment and HCC surveillance. To refine the management of CHB, previous studies focused on identifying the at‐risk populations and predictors for adverse outcomes using conventional statistical methods. With the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI), there is further room to improve different aspects of screening and management. For instance, generative AI, such as large language models (LLMs), has been proven to have the ability to answer different clinical questions, assisting patients' and physicians' decision on various clinical scenarios. Different machine learning and deep learning models have also been developed to assess for liver fibrosis, as well as to aid segmentation of liver structures and detection of focal liver lesions through various imaging modalities. While different AI models have shown superior performance compared to those developed through traditional statistical models, the lack of standardized datasets in training cohorts and the unresolved concerns of hallucination of false information in LLMs pose challenges on applying AI in the current management of CHB, in which further studies are required to adopt AI into daily clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-technical skills are important for perioperative patient safety. The Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills (SPLINTS) system provides a structured framework for observing scrub practitioners' non-technical skills, but its clinical application in Japan remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical feasibility and preliminary reliability of the revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills in actual operating room practice. METHODS: Seven Certified Nurses in Perioperative Nursing used the revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills to observe and rate 18 scrub nurses. Clinical observability, internal consistency, and exploratory correlations among the three Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills categories were examined. RESULTS: Cronbach's alpha was 0.967 for Situation Awareness, 0.963 for Communication and Teamwork, and 0.949 for Task Management. Some behaviours received not-rated responses, suggesting that observability may depend on the surgical context. Correlations among the three categories were positive (ρ = 0.47-0.81). CONCLUSIONS: The revised Japanese Scrub Practitioners' List of Intraoperative Non-Technical Skills supported structured observation of non-technical skills in actual surgical practice. These preliminary findings support further evaluation and practical implementation in Japanese perioperative settings.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, raising methodological and ethical questions for qualitative research instruction. This article examines how we, three experienced qualitative research instructors, integrated GAI tools into our graduate-level research methods courses. Our pedagogical approach to integrating GAI tools is situated within the broader literature on GAI in higher education and qualitative research instruction, emphasizing active learning and technological reflexivity. Our work is also guided by Ethan Mollick’s artificial intelligence (AI) principles from Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI. Using reflective narrative case examples, we demonstrate how Mollick’s principles guided ethical and methodologically responsive integration of GAI, challenged assumptions about rigor and trustworthiness, and reconfigured instructor–student relationships. We conclude by highlighting tensions between efficiency, inclusion, and epistemic responsibility and implications for qualitative research education.

Data visualization is mandatory for different applications, such data interpretation, exploratory analysis, pattern identification, etc. It is rapidly used in the domain of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML), healthcare and medical analytics, cybersecurity, finance, IoT, etc. Although it is effectively used in several areas, but it has some issues such as large volume of data, choosing the right visualization technique, data quality, user interpretation, etc. In this paper, five visualization methods are used to illustrate a compact multi-view visualization in the form of an analytical. Finally, the results show that each chart illustrates a specific insight. Among all visualizations, scatter visualization provides richer information with the context of feature relationship and class separability.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: This technical note presents a unified, public‑facing explanation of four major architectures used to understand how artificial intelligence systems interact with human meaning: NDH‑Constellation, UMM, UMA, and the Sovereignty Library. Each of these architectures operates in a different domain—mathematical, reflective, or constitutional—and this work shows how they can coexist without collapsing into one another. NDH‑Constellation is a mathematical system designed to analyze stability, drift, and coherence in complex AI behavior. It provides tools for understanding how meaning moves through a model without absorbing human narratives or collapsing under interpretive pressure. This property—NDH’s ability to remain contextual without losing stability—is increasingly important for AI interpretability, where systems must adapt to different users and environments while still remaining predictable and safe. UMM and UMA form the reflective layer. UMM defines the basic building blocks of reflective meaning, while UMA governs how those blocks move, interact, and unfold during human–AI communication. Together, they create a structured, non‑coercive environment that preserves ambiguity and prevents over‑interpretation. This is essential for designing AI systems that respect human agency and avoid forcing meaning where none exists. The Sovereignty Library provides the constitutional layer. It defines dignity, relational meaning, and witness sovereignty—principles that ensure human meaning is handled respectfully and without compression. These constitutional invariants prevent AI systems from reducing or overriding human narratives, especially in sensitive contexts such as trauma, identity, or transnational repression. A central contribution of this work is the concept of cross‑architecture resonance: the idea that different systems can align at their boundaries without merging their internal rules. NDH resonates with the Sovereignty Library at the structural level, but their invariants remain separate. UMM and UMA resonate through container‑and‑movement alignment. NDH does not resonate with UMM or UMA, which prevents mathematical behavior from being mistaken for reflective or constitutional meaning. This separation is crucial for AI interpretability. It ensures that mathematical diagnostics do not override human dignity, and that reflective meaning does not distort mathematical clarity. By keeping these domains distinct, hybrid AI systems can remain stable, interpretable, and ethically grounded even under complex or shifting epistemic conditions. This note is presented as a preprint‑style technical design document to support ongoing research in AI interpretability, constitutional AI, hybrid architectures, and human–AI meaning systems. It includes appendices detailing operator algebra, ontology tables, movement systems, constitutional invariants, and diagnostic criteria, offering a structured foundation for future work in both technical and human‑centered AI research. --- Acknowledgment of Origin and Research Fork This technical note arises from an independent research fork of the original Sovereignty Library, created by Christopher Chenoweth and Peter Lodri as part of the 8b research project. The original project is publicly available at: The analysis presented here does not modify, extend, or reinterpret the Sovereignty Library’s constitutional ontology. Instead, it examines the library’s invariants, dignity manifold, and witness‑sovereignty structures as part of a broader cross‑architecture study involving NDH‑Constellation, UMM, and UMA. No collaboration or communication occurred between the author of this technical note and the creators of the Sovereignty Library. The work is a research‑driven architectural analysis, not an official extension of the original project.

documents.abstract: Artikel ini membahas pergeseran paradigma evaluasi kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence atau AI) dari sekadar mengukur skor akurasi model menuju pembangunan kerangka akuntabilitas operasional dalam konteks pengambilan keputusan hukum dan administrasi publik. Mengacu pada NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) dan OWASP GenAI Security Project, tulisan ini merumuskan kerangka keselamatan komprehensif yang mencakup: Model Risiko Berbasis Probabilitas Bersyarat: Memisahkan probabilitas galat model, probabilitas kegagalan kontrol, dan besarnya dampak kerugian (expected loss). Batas Statistik Uji Evaluasi: Menganalisis batasan uji statistik berbasis Rule of Three dan Clopper-Pearson ((N \geq 30.000) untuk target galat 0,01%), serta penanganan common-mode failures dan cluster correlation. Kontrol Struktural dan Integrasi Sumber: Membedakan integritas, autentisitas, kemutakhiran, dan kelengkapan sumber hukum (JDIH/SNI), serta mitigasi bias otomatisasi (automation bias). Matriks Keputusan Operasional: Menetapkan empat status operasional, yaitu Status A (Operasi Penuh), Status L (Penggunaan Terbatas), Status B (Penangguhan), dan Status C (Penolakan Fungsi Otonom), berdasarkan analisis akar penyebab (Root Cause Analysis atau RCA).

documents.abstract: Cognitive fatigue during 12-hr shifts can reduce attention, slow responses, and increase error risk in safety-critical healthcare and manufacturing settings. This study evaluated a multimodal wearable system for detecting fatigue and delivering timely micro-break prompts. Fifty shift workers wore sensors measuring photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, and inertial movement during normal work. These signals were combined with brief micro-task measures and analyzed using a gradient boosting fusion model. Ground truth indicators included Psychomotor Vigilance Task lapses and self-reported fatigue. The model achieved an AUC of approximately 0.82, indicating useful field-based detection performance. Workers receiving fatigue-triggered micro-break prompts showed approximately 21% fewer late-shift vigilance lapses than controls, without measurable productivity loss. Individual calibration improved model reliability and prompt timing across workers. Participants also emphasized privacy, transparency, and data governance as essential for adoption. Overall, the findings support wearable, individualized, lowburden fatigue management to improve vigilance during extended shifts in diverse real-world occupational environments.

The need to reduce carbon emissions, manage scarce resources, and improve operational efficiency has increased interest in digital technologies for sustainable operations. This PRISMA 2020-guided, single-reviewer systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), data analytics, digital twins, and related technologies are associated with sustainability outcomes in organizational operations, and under which implementation conditions those outcomes are reported. Four databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, and IEEE Xplore) were searched on 15 March 2026 for peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 2023 and March 2026. The review log records 420 records identified, 110 duplicates removed, 310 records screened, 95 full-text reports assessed, and 42 studies retained. These counts are arithmetically consistent, but screening, eligibility assessment, and data extraction were performed by one reviewer, the protocol was not prospectively registered, and no inter-rater statistic exists; the 42-study set therefore should not be regarded as independently verified. Because the studies use different baselines, system boundaries, and outcome definitions, no pooled estimate and no cross-study percentage range is reported. Quantitative results are presented only where they can be traced to a named primary study, for example a 4.21% reduction in energy consumption from a physics-guided neural network in two industrial case studies [1], a 7.62% reduction in automated-guided-vehicle energy consumption from digital-twin-based scheduling [2], a 51.5% observed reduction in energy consumption at a single manufacturing machine from IIoT energy monitoring [3], and a model-predicted 6.0% energy-consumption reduction from a machine-learning model applied to a pelleting press [4]; each is treated as a context-specific observation rather than a general effect size. The review also examines life-cycle burdens, rebound effects, e-waste, data-center electricity and water demand, workforce implications, digital inequality, and critical-mineral supply risks, drawing on adjacent literature outside the 42-study set. A Digital-Operations-Sustainability (DOS) framework is proposed as a conceptual model whose five propositions are hypotheses for future testing, not validated relationships. Priorities for future work include dual-reviewer, prospectively registered evidence synthesis; standardized sustainability indicators; integration of AI with life cycle assessment; longitudinal validation; and evidence from small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and developing economies.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Today, cloud computing, edge intelligence, microservices, serverless computing, and federated artificial intelligence rely on distributed systems for computing resources. The growing need for sustainability studies is complicated by the intervening variables surrounding sustainability, which span such areas as software architecture, orchestration, network components, heterogeneous hardware, cooling, electricity generation, and hardware production. Moreover, AI presents a further complication to the sustainability discourse because it represents both a rapidly growing workload as well as a means of optimizing resource allocation, forecasting, scheduling, and controlling resources. This systematic integrative review covers findings until September 2026 related to sustainability in distributed systems. Reporting was guided by PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S principles for scope definition, concepts searched, and eligibility, extraction, interpretation, and synthesis processes, although a full PRISMA flow diagram could not be reconstructed because database export-level logs were unavailable. The final corpus included 96 sources, including over 80 peer-reviewed studies from published articles, standards, and measurement reports. This synthesis identifies five groups of best practices for the application/model layer, namely demand reduction; resource proportionality and consolidation; edge-cloud placement and workload shifting; carbon- and thermal-aware infrastructure management; and measurement/governance based on the principle of functional units and life-cycle boundaries. Apart from that, it has been discovered that energy is still the primary measure while operational carbon, embodied emissions, water, network effects, and hardware life cycle are still measured in less consistent manner. The frameworks currently available, including sustainability models, Sustainability Awareness Framework, Green Software Measurement Model, Software Carbon Intensity, and new green federated-learning frameworks address various parts of the problem but seldom provide a complete cross-layer measurement-and-control cycle at all. To fill in this gap, the review proposes SAIDS (Sustainability Aware AI for Distributed Systems) framework, which involves Measure-Attribute-Predict-Optimize-Verify-Report stages and relies on service, reliability, privacy, cost, and life-cycle dimensions.

Biodiversity genomics research increasingly relies on multi-view visualization tools to support comparative analyses spanning species identification, evolutionary factors, hierarchical taxonomic relationships, wildlife forensics, population structure analysis, and conservation planning, which place distinct demands on visualization design. Despite the growing prevalence of multi-view layouts in the genomics domain, systematic understanding of how they support domain-specific biological goals through task abstractions remains limited. This systematic literature review addresses these gaps by establishing a domain-task mapping framework that explicitly connects biodiversity genomics biological goals to visualization task abstractions through an evidence-based software engineering approach. Applying a dual-task taxonomy that includes genomic-specific tasks and comparative actions, this review analyzed 34 papers identified through a structured search across five databases, using active-learning-assisted screening and an LLM-assisted data-extraction workflow. The results identify characteristic task-flow structures for four biological goals using Markov chain analysis and summarize their universal and unique structural patterns. Furthermore, five challenge-solution themes are documented across the included papers, encompassing visualization, tool features, tasks, data integration, and user interface and experience. These findings provide evidence-based guidance for visualization designers creating biodiversity genomics tools and bioinformaticians seeking to understand how multi-view designs support complex analytical workflows.

ABSTRACT: 本文延續作者對「囍—𩺰—龖」的文化思考,將古字「龖」重新詮釋為 Dragon²(亦寫作 Dragon2)。囍象徵新婚之喜,𩺰象徵夫妻無論順境逆境皆相伴一生;龖則將關懷由家庭延伸至世界。在本文所採用的麻將規則中,「雙龍抱」指由兩對相同順子構成的組合,共含四副順子,每對中的兩副順子花色與數序相同。作者借其「抱而不鬥」的意象,將兩龍比喻為具有全球影響力的中國與美國,寄託兩國相互尊重、和平共存的願望。這是作者提出的跨文化和平隱喻,並非將龍視為美國固有的國家象徵。作者於龍年出生於中國,1949年遷至臺灣,後赴美求學、成家與工作。中國承載其出生、文化與早年記憶,臺灣見證其成長與求學,美國則承載其深造、事業與家庭生活。這段跨越海峽與太平洋的生命歷程,使中美關係成為與自身及家人命運相連的切身議題。本文比較「雙龍爭珠」「雙龍戲珠」「雙龍抱」與「雙龍護珠」的意象:若明珠代表霸權,兩龍可能陷入零和競爭;若明珠代表地球,兩龍便肩負共同守護的責任。文章進一步借用工程系統中的回饋、穩定與失控概念,闡述核戰無真正贏家的警示,主張中美競而不戰、強而有制、和而不同,並在氣候變遷、公共衛生、人工智慧安全與核風險降低等領域推動合作。和平的意義亦須落實於平民百姓的生活,使家庭免於戰亂、人民安居樂業、世代得以延續。「龖」為既有古漢字,由兩個繁體「龍」左右並列而成。本文賦予其「雙龍抱,雙吉祥,共築人間仙境」的文化新意,以兩龍相擁、彼此尊重,象徵雙重吉祥、和諧共存與天下太平。此一意涵及其中的中美合作寓意,均屬作者的現代文化詮釋,而非「龖」字的傳統字典釋義; 關鍵詞:龖;Dragon²;Dragon2;雙龍抱;麻將文化;囍;𩺰;中美關係;生命書寫;系統工程;核風險降低;世界和平;和諧共存;天下太平;雙重吉祥;平民福祉;中美合作; ABSTRACT: This article continues the author's cultural reflections on the sequence 囍–𩺰–龖, reinterpreting the ancient Chinese character 龖 as Dragon² (also written as Dragon2). 囍 symbolizes the joy of marriage, while 𩺰 represents lifelong companionship through prosperity and adversity. 龖 extends this concern from the family to the world. In the mahjong rules adopted here, "Double Dragon Embrace" consists of two pairs of identical sequences—four sequences in total, with the two sequences in each pair matching in both suit and numerical order. Drawing on the image of "embracing rather than fighting," the author uses the two dragons as a metaphor for China and the United States, two globally influential powers, expressing the hope that they will respect each other and coexist peacefully. This is a cross-cultural metaphor for peace proposed by the author, not a claim that the dragon is a traditional national symbol of the United States. Born in China in the Year of the Dragon, the author moved to Taiwan in 1949 and later pursued further education, established a family, and developed his career in the United States. China holds his birthplace, cultural roots, and early memories; Taiwan shaped his upbringing and education; and the United States became the setting for his advanced studies, career, and family life. This life journey across the Taiwan Strait and the Pacific makes U.S.–China relations a deeply personal concern connected to his own and his family's future. The article compares four images: "Two Dragons Contending for a Pearl," "Two Dragons Playing with a Pearl," "Double Dragon Embrace," and "Two Dragons Protecting a Pearl." If the pearl represents hegemony, the dragons may become trapped in zero-sum competition; if it represents the Earth, they share a responsibility to protect it. Drawing further on the engineering concepts of feedback, stability, and loss of control, the article emphasizes that nuclear war has no true winners. It advocates competition without warfare, strength exercised with restraint, and harmony without uniformity, alongside cooperation on climate change, public health, artificial intelligence safety, and nuclear risk reduction. Peace must also take concrete form in the lives of ordinary people, allowing families to live free from war, communities to thrive, and future generations to flourish. The character 龖 consists of two traditional Chinese 龍 characters placed side by side. The author gives it a new cultural meaning: "Two dragons embrace, bringing paired blessings and together creating an earthly paradise." Their embrace and mutual respect symbolize shared auspiciousness, harmonious coexistence, and peace under heaven. These meanings, including the association with U.S.–China cooperation, are the author's contemporary cultural interpretation rather than traditional dictionary definitions of 龖. KEYWORDS: 龖; Dragon²; Dragon2; Double Dragon Embrace; mahjong culture; 囍; 𩺰; U.S.–China relations; life writing; systems engineering; nuclear risk reduction; world peace; harmonious coexistence; peace under heaven; paired blessings; well-being of ordinary people; U.S.–China cooperation

Abstract Educational artificial intelligence (AI) does not become high-risk under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act 2024 merely because it is used in schools. Its classification depends on the function it performs within the educational process: whether it supports learning formatively, or whether it evaluates learning outcomes in ways that affect a student’s educational trajectory. This distinction is especially unstable in adaptive generative AI systems, where the same interactional features that make a tool pedagogically useful may, if repurposed or institutionally relied upon, move it towards the assessment logic of Annex III, point 3(b) of the AI Act. This paper uses Estonia’s AI Leap initiative as an early test case for that boundary. It develops four claims. First, the boundary between formative tutoring and high-risk assessment is conditional and dynamic, rather than inherent in the technology itself. Second, the profiling rule in Article 6(3) of the AI Act is best understood as an anti-derogation trigger: it does not independently bring a system within Annex III, but once an educational AI system falls within Annex III, profiling prevents reliance on the derogation from high-risk classification. Third, the initiative exposes a value-chain asymmetry characteristic of public-sector educational deployments built on third-party general-purpose AI models, in which downstream actors may acquire compliance responsibilities without full technical control. Fourth, Section 20¹ amendment to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act (Estonia) 2010 provides an unusually concrete national-law basis for educational AI processing, but it cannot by itself resolve the data-protection problems created by open-input generative systems, especially the incidental capture of special-category and third-party data. The paper concludes that the initiative’s regulatory significance lies less in its present classification than in the governance conditions needed to prevent functional drift and mitigate the data-protection risks created by open-ended student inputs.

documents.abstract: People often make different decisions depending on whether outcomes are described as gains or losses, even when the numbers are the same. This study examined how the presentation of information influenced decisions. Participants completed a series of decision-making scenarios across real-world contexts, including military operations, disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and infrastructure failures. In each case, they chose between a guaranteed outcome and a risky alternative. Outcomes were shown either as text or as visual displays called icon arrays, which represented individuals as simple graphics. When outcomes were presented in text, participants showed classic framing effects: they preferred safe options when outcomes were framed as gains and riskier options when framed as losses. However, when the same information was shown using icon arrays, this difference disappeared and moved toward preferring the safe option. These findings indicate that visualizing risk can reduce bias in decision-making. Improving how risk information is presented may help people make more informed and consistent choices.

Small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises form the backbone of industrial economies worldwide, yet they consistently struggle to monitor energy use, control energy cost, and meet sustainability targets because affordable, integrated decision-support tools remain scarce. This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven digital twin for energy optimization that unifies, within a single low-cost platform, five capabilities that prior studies address only in isolation: interpretable regression of energy against production, ensemble and recurrent Machine Learning (ML) models benchmarked for demand prediction and forecasting, generator-activation alerting, statistical anomaly detection, and a what-if scenario simulator with a decision-support dashboard. The framework ingests daily production volume together with grid-supplied and diesel-generator energy from an operating facility and derives Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for energy efficiency, Energy Per Unit of production (EPU), operating cost, and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. Linear and quadratic regression models link production to energy demand and are scored with the coefficient of determination (R2) and Root-Mean-Square error (RMSE); a Random Forest (RF) regressor, an exploratory RF generator-activation alert, and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for next-day forecasting are benchmarked against these interpretable baselines; because only six of the 59 valid daily observations were generator-active, the RF alert is not treated as a validated classifier. The principal novelty lies in integrating these complementary methods within one vendor-neutral digital twin aimed at resource-constrained enterprises. On a real case-study dataset, quadratic regression captures the production–energy relationship more closely than the linear baseline, and a load-shifting recommendation avoids generator use on the peak-demand day, reducing both cost and CO 2 emissions, while a 50% reduction in generator reliance yields substantial additional savings. A cross-validation study further shows that, in this small-data regime, higher-capacity ensemble and recurrent models do not improve out-of-sample accuracy over interpretable regression—an instructive finding that motivates the framework’s emphasis on transparent, deployable models for resource-constrained enterprises.

documents.abstract: This study examined the use of Google Classroom-supported ESL lessons to enhance Year 5 pupils’ intrinsic motivation in learning English at a primary school in Pendang, Kedah. The study was conducted in response to concerns about pupils’ limited motivation and participation in English lessons, as well as the need for more structured use of digital learning platforms in primary ESL classrooms. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the study focused on three dimensions of intrinsic motivation: interest and enjoyment, perceived competence, and pressure and tension. An action research design was employed with 30 Year 5 ESL pupils. Over four weeks, the pupils participated in Google Classroom-supported ESL lessons that included structured vocabulary tasks, interactive activities, and teacher feedback. Data were collected using selected subscales from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory before and after the intervention. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The findings showed a statistically significant but modest change in pupils’ intrinsic motivation after the intervention. These findings suggest that Google Classroom may support pupils’ motivation when it is used as part of guided, interactive, and teacher-supported ESL lessons rather than as a stand-alone digital platform. The study contributes classroom-based evidence on the use of Google Classroom in Malaysian primary ESL education and highlights the importance of structured digital activities in supporting pupils’ motivation to learn English.

Dynamic Positioning (DP) systems are widely used in offshore operations such as drilling, subsea construction, cable laying, offshore renewable energy support, and remotely operated vehicle (ROV) operations. As offshore activities become increasingly dependent on DP capability, failures in DP systems may result in operational disruption, safety concerns, and environmental exposure. Although advances in automation and redundancy have improved DP system reliability, the offshore industry continues to report DP incidents and undesired events. This paper reviews DP station-keeping events reported by the International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) between 2018 and 2024. The reported percentages reflect descriptive compositions of voluntary submissions rather than incident rates or statistically generalizable temporal trends. The review focuses on recurring reported patterns related to thruster and propulsion failures, electrical faults, position reference problems, computer-related failures, and human factors. The review also discusses the operational and environmental implications of DP failures during offshore activities. Loss of position, reduced redundancy, and degraded vessel capability may increase the risk of collision, subsea equipment damage, operational downtime, and other offshore safety concerns. The paper also highlights the ongoing contribution of electrical and human factors to reported DP events. Finally, the paper discusses several approaches that may improve the resilience of future DP operations, including predictive maintenance, decision-support systems, and AI-based monitoring technologies. The findings suggest that DP failures should be considered not only as technical malfunctions, but also as part of a broader offshore operational and environmental risk management issue.

Purpose This paper develops a conceptual methodological framework for governing the use of artificial intelligence in the grounded theory. It addresses the risk that AI-generated outputs may be mistaken for qualitative evidence, interpretation or theory. Design/methodology/approach The paper synthesizes grounded theory traditions, computational grounded theory, large language model supported coding, human in the loop research, qualitative trustworthiness and critical AI scholarship. It develops a validation gate framework and uses a worked methodological vignette to show how AI suggestions can be documented, checked and bounded. Findings The paper argues that AI can support retrieval, organization, candidate coding, comparison and adversarial audit, but cannot authorize meaning, categories or theory. It identifies seven validation gates and four modes of AI use: assistive, dialogic, generative and adversarial audit. Originality/value The paper differentiates epistemic governance from reflexivity, trustworthiness, auditability and human in the loop design by focusing on the epistemic status of AI outputs before they enter the analytic record. It offers operational pass criteria for preserving theoretical sensitivity, reflexivity, auditability and researcher accountability when grounded theory is scaled through AI.

documents.abstract: Responsible AI principles like fairness, accountability, and transparency are built on Western institutional assumptions yet exported as universal standards. We systematically reviewed (N=41) studies from underrepresented regions to identify locally prioritized values and their tensions with dominant discourse. Three frictions emerged: epistemic (whose knowledge counts as ethical expertise), contextual (whether abstract principles survive local conditions), and infrastructural (how resource asymmetries constrain value realization). Our findings show Global Majority scholarship does not simply add new values to the list. They reconfigure ethics through lived experience by redefining the core logic: fairness shifts from individual parity to collective well-being; transparency shifts from technical disclosure to relational trust but bounded by protocol and custom; and accountability shifts from top-down audit to distributed responsibility shaped by labor conditions and data sovereignty. This study advocates for centering epistemic pluralism as a prerequisite for ethically legitimate AI governance rather than treating these frictions as implementation failures.

documents.abstract: Source-grounded generative AI assistants can improve access to disciplinary literature, but citations do not ensure technical correctness. We evaluated two textile- and offset-printing assistants in Google NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), using 20 controlled prompts per assistant. One subject-matter expert rated technical accuracy, completeness, source support, and contextualization and manually checked citations. Mean overall scores were 4.73/5 and 4.61/5, respectively; because prompt sets differed, these are descriptive, not comparative. Source support exceeded technical accuracy in 35 of 40 original responses. In eight explicitly prompted knowledge-boundary tests, six responses showed appropriate abstention and two showed abstention with reservations; this evaluates prompted handling, not spontaneous recognition. Of seven repeated pairs with preserved identical wording, six received unchanged overall scores (mean absolute difference, 0.036/5); content comparison found recurring errors and differences across the ten pairs, although three offset pairs were only same-topic comparisons. A recurring textile error labeled source-reported heat-setting temperatures as glass-transition temperatures; a reported fabric-temperature rise applies only to vat-dye all-in cotton printing in saturated steam. With one expert evaluator and 15 original offset prompts preserved only as topic labels, this is an exploratory case study, not a validated benchmark. Student learning outcomes were not assessed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Ergonomic research in workspace design has largely been limited to chair-seated and standing work postures. However, a majority of the global workforce is employed in the informal economy, especially in parts of Asia and Africa where floor-based work postures are dominant. This pilot study analyzed floor-based work of 10 workers engaged in 5 occupations–fishmongers, poultry butchers, vegetable sellers, potters, cobblers—in a bazaar in New Delhi, India. Video analysis of 10-min segments revealed that floor-based workers performed tasks within dynamically negotiated, multi-level worksurfaces, rather than fixed-height workstations. Workers employed postural strategies including auxiliary limb engagement, asymmetrical load distribution, and continuous spinal reconfiguration to reshape the workspace geometries. Joint angle estimates ranged from 110° to 130° in knee and 90° to 120° in hip flexion, respectively. Preliminary findings suggest that floor-based work operates through an adaptive spatio-temporal logic distinct from the paradigm of chair-seated and standing work postures.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Smart meters and Internet of Things (IoT) modems are now essential for remote monitoring and management in energy distribution systems, but they also widen the attack surface. Vulnerabilities span the hardware, firmware, communication, and data-management layers, and this study addresses them with a five-layer security and hardening framework based on the zero-trust model. Seven mechanisms are integrated within a single architecture: endpoint hardware protection, secure boot, mutual authentication, network micro-segmentation, operational command verification, artificial intelligence-based anomaly detection, and privacy-preserving data aggregation. The framework was evaluated in a laboratory testbed across eight scenarios: physical tampering, malicious firmware, unauthorized connection, network scanning, denial-of-service, replay attacks, low-rate stealthy network anomalies, and consumer profiling via data exposure. Cryptographic key zeroization had a mean latency of 14.2 ± 1.1 ms, unauthorized network traffic was blocked according to the configured security policies, and the SIEM alert associated with replay rejection was generated within 127.08 ms. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based time-series model achieved 95.73% accuracy with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9696. For the privacy layer, anonymized load-profile data obtained from field-deployed smart meters operating within the Advanced Metering Infrastructure of Dicle Electricity Distribution Inc. were used. The MCFE hourly aggregate of the 11 complete meter profiles matched the plaintext reference with zero error in all 24 hourly slots. These laboratory results support the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed layered design for smart-meter and IoT-modem infrastructures under the tested conditions.

Organizations increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve strategic planning, operational efficiency, and sustainability. However, conventional machine learning models often lack transparency, limiting managerial trust, accountability, and the practical adoption of AI-driven decisions. This study proposes an explainable AI (XAI) framework that integrates predictive analytics, interpretable machine learning, and sustainability indicators to support transparent, reliable, and evidence-based decision-making across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions. The proposed framework combines Random Forest, XGBoost, and Explainable Boosting Machines with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). Evaluation uses a benchmark dataset containing operational performance, resource consumption, organizational efficiency, and environmental indicators. Comparative experiments assess predictive accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), explanation consistency, decision latency, computational cost, and sustainability performance. Baseline models include Logistic Regression, conventional Random Forest, and XGBoost without explanation mechanisms. Ablation studies examine the individual contributions of interpretability and sustainability-aware optimization. The experimental evaluation is designed to determine whether the proposed framework improves predictive reliability, explanation quality, and sustainability-aware decisions compared with conventional approaches. Quantitative reporting will include percentage improvements in predictive performance, reductions in decision latency and resource consumption, and explanation stability across repeated experiments. Qualitative analysis will assess managerial understandability, perceived trustworthiness, fairness, and practical implementation challenges. Numerical outcomes will be reported only after experiments are completed, avoiding unsupported performance claims. The proposed framework establishes a comparative approach for integrating explainability, predictive intelligence, and sustainability into organizational decision-making. By connecting model predictions with transparent explanations and measurable sustainability indicators, the framework aims to strengthen accountability, operational effectiveness, and responsible technology adoption. Future validation across multiple industries will establish its generalizability and practical value. Keywords: Predictive Analytics; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Sustainable Decision-Making; Interpretable Machine Learning; Organizational Intelligence.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research, environmental sustainability, healthcare, and intelligent infrastructure. However, conventional AI approaches often lack interpretability, cross-domain adaptability, and transparent decision-making. This study proposes an explainable multidisciplinary AI framework integrating predictive analytics, explainable AI (XAI), and multi-criteria decision analysis to support sustainable innovation across diverse research domains. The proposed framework combines Random Forest, XGBoost, and Explainable Boosting Machines with SHAP-based feature attribution and multi-criteria decision analysis. A comparative evaluation design considers environmental sustainability, healthcare, and intelligent infrastructure as representative application domains. Models are assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), explanation fidelity, computational latency, and decision consistency. Baseline comparisons include conventional machine learning without explanations, explainable models without decision optimization, and the integrated framework. Sustainability indicators, interpretability, computational efficiency, and decision robustness are incorporated into a unified evaluation protocol. Performance is compared using consistent data-splitting procedures, domain-specific metrics, and sensitivity analysis. The proposed framework establishes a measurable evaluation strategy for determining whether integrated explainability and decision optimization improve predictive reliability and practical decision support. Quantitative outcomes will include differences in predictive performance, explanation fidelity, latency, and decision consistency across models and domains. Qualitative analysis will examine stakeholder interpretability, cross-domain adaptability, transparency, and the relevance of generated recommendations. Numerical improvements will be reported only after empirical experimentation. This research advances a unified approach to explainable, multidisciplinary AI by connecting predictive intelligence with transparent, sustainability-oriented decision-making. Its comparative design supports reproducible assessment of accuracy, interpretability, efficiency, and robustness. The framework offers a foundation for responsible AI deployment across emerging research domains while highlighting the need for domain-specific validation, representative datasets, and human oversight. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Multidisciplinary Machine Learning; Sustainable Innovation; Intelligent Decision-Making; SHAP Interpretability.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Partially automated driving systems require drivers to remain cognitively engaged and prepared to respond to unexpected roadway hazards despite reduced direct vehicle control. In rural driving, low visibility and sudden animal crossings pose unique safety challenges to driver readiness and response capability. This study presents an exploratory multimodal machine learning framework for hazard-response classification under semi-automated rural driving. Using a high-fidelity driving simulator, EEG, eye activity, behavioral, and subjective workload data were acquired under manual and Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS)-supported conditions. Pre-hazard event-level features were evaluated using logistic regression, random forest, and multilayer perceptron classifiers with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Random Forest achieved the highest mean classification accuracy, although performance was constrained by class imbalance and limited sensitivity to brake events. Feature-importance analysis identified SART situation-awareness score as the most influential feature, followed by NASA-TLX workload, pupil-diameter change, and EEG-derived measures. These findings support multimodal hazard-response classification for future driver-readiness modeling.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed software engineering by introducing intelligent systems that support automation and creativity throughout the development lifecycle.AI-assisted UI/UX design tools, in particular, can generate interface components, create prototypes, and recommend design improvements, offering opportunities to enhance productivity and accelerate development.However, adoption among software professionals remains uncertain, as AI-based creative systems introduce unique challenges related to trust, reliability, transparency, and ethics.This study investigates the factors influencing adoption intention of AI-assisted design tools among software professionals using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM).The proposed model integrates Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, and Trust in AI, Creativity Support, and Ethical Concerns, with Attitude Toward AI-Assisted Design Tools as a mediating construct.A quantitative, cross-sectional survey will collect data from software engineers, UI/UX designers, developers, and computing students.Analysis will employ descriptive statistics, reliability and validity tests, correlation, and PLS-SEM.This research aims to contribute empirical insights into AI adoption behaviour, supporting organizations and educators in developing strategies for integrating AI-assisted design technologies into modern software workflows.

Abstract This article examines fair and trustworthy artificial intelligence in public administration, presenting Estonia as the main case and EU law as the wider legal frame. It builds on the EquiTech project, which has been successfully co-implemented by the TalTech Department of Law and its project partners. The project materials, including training materials for public servants and data scientists, the project proposal, and related academic work, form an important empirical and normative basis for the article. The central claim is that fairness in public-sector artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be reduced to technical accuracy, general transparency, or compliance with a single legal instrument. Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell’s work on why fairness cannot be automated is the paper’s main theoretical anchor. Their concept of contextual equality helps explain why EU non-discrimination law does not translate easily into fixed fairness metrics, even though statistical evidence remains necessary. In the Estonian setting, this problem is visible in the gap between an advanced digital state and a still developing framework for assessing bias and discrimination risks across the full lifecycle of automated decision-making. The article argues that trustworthy public-sector AI requires legal authority, data governance, bias assessment, meaningful human oversight, administrative contestability, and institutional capacity. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act is a major step in this direction, but it cannot by itself solve the legal and practical problems raised by algorithmic discrimination in public administration.
